How to Use This Book

This book is written so that you can prepare the whole of Section B of MTE 4033 without opening the lecture slides. Each chapter follows the same order:

  1. Theory: full explanations of every idea on the KMS slides, rewritten as exam-ready paragraphs and point lists.
  2. Derivations: every equation derived step by step, with nothing skipped.
  3. Solved past questions: every Section B question from the 2022, 2023 and 2024 term finals, answered in full at the length the marks call for.
  4. Practice numericals: the past papers set almost no numericals, so worked problems have been written for each model (slip, stopping distance, cruise response, CAN timing, yaw rate, regeneration) in case one is set.

Appendix: Formula Sheet, Keywords and Answer Key

1. Introduction to Advanced Vehicle Technology & Autotronics ★★★

1.1 What is Advanced Vehicle Technology (AVT)?

Definition
Advanced Vehicle Technology (AVT) is the application of new, cutting-edge technologies to the design and development of vehicles. Its aim is to improve their performance, safety, efficiency and sustainability.

The two standard textbook definitions quoted in the lecture are:

  • Heinz Heisler (Advanced Vehicle Technology): AVT covers the design and development of vehicles that use new and innovative technologies to improve fuel efficiency, reduce emissions, improve safety features and increase comfort and convenience for the driver and passengers.
  • Rajesh Rajamani (Vehicle Dynamics and Control): AVT is the study of advanced technologies related to vehicles, including advanced propulsion systems, vehicle dynamics and control, and vehicle safety systems. Its goal is to improve the overall performance of vehicles while reducing their impact on the environment.

AVT therefore brings together four areas: (i) propulsion (efficient IC engines, hybrid, electric, fuel cell), (ii) vehicle dynamics and control (ABS, TCS, ESP, cruise control, steering), (iii) safety (active and passive), and (iv) comfort, connectivity and autonomy (infotainment, ADAS, self-driving). What these areas share is electronics and software. The Bosch figure shown in the lecture (“Proportion of electrics/electronics in the motor vehicle”) shows the share of E/E in the value of a car rising steadily from a few percent in the 1970s to roughly a third or more today. In electric and autonomous vehicles the share is even higher.

1.2 Autotronics

Definition of Autotronics (write this in the exam)
Autotronics combines Automotive and Electronics. It is the branch of engineering that deals with electronic systems used in vehicles: engine management, ignition, transmission control, braking and stability control, radio, telematics, in-car entertainment and others. In practice, autotronics systems are automotive embedded systems: distributed networks of microcontroller-based control units (ECUs), sensors and actuators, connected by in-vehicle networks such as CAN and LIN.

1.2.1 Classification of automotive electronics by domain

Automotive embedded systems are distributed systems. They are grouped by the domain of the vehicle they serve:

DomainWhat it doesTypical examples
1. Engine electronicsReal-time control of combustion, emissions and engine auxiliaries. This domain has some of the tightest timing deadlines in the car.Fuel injection, ignition timing, throttle, turbo boost, OBD
2. Chassis electronicsMonitors and actively controls braking, traction and stabilityABS, TCS, EBD, ESP, parking assistance
3. Transmission electronicsShift scheduling and clutch/torque-converter controlAutomatic transmission control unit (TCU), CVT, DCT control
4. Automotive safetyAvoids accidents (active safety) or reduces their effects (passive safety)Airbags, seat-belt pretensioners, TPMS
5. Driver assistance (ADAS)Helps the driver perceive the surroundings and actLane assist, blind-spot detection, adaptive cruise, park assist, pre-collision assist
6. Passenger comfortClimate and convenience functionsAutomatic climate control, power seats, windows, mirrors
7. InfotainmentInformation and entertainmentNavigation, audio, phone connectivity, telematics
8. Electronic integrated cockpitCombines displays and controls into one digital driver interfaceDigital instrument cluster, head-up display, central touch screen

1.3 Engine Electronics: Functions of the Engine ECU

The engine control unit is one of the most demanding electronic parts of a car. The engine is a very fast, complex process: at 6000 rpm the crankshaft turns once every 10 ms. Injection and spark events must therefore be computed and timed to within microseconds, which makes the engine ECU a hard real-time system. It controls:

FunctionExplanation
Fuel injection rate controlCalculates injector opening time from air mass, engine speed, temperature and lambda (O₂) feedback, to hold the chosen air–fuel ratio (≈14.7:1 for petrol).
Ignition system controlSets the spark advance from speed, load and knock-sensor signals, for maximum torque without knocking.
Emission controlClosed-loop lambda control, EGR valve, catalyst heating and evaporative purge, to meet emission norms.
Turbocharger controlRegulates boost pressure through a wastegate or variable-geometry vanes.
Cooling system controlSwitches electric fans and electronic thermostats from coolant temperature.
OBD (On-Board Diagnostics)Watches sensors and actuators, stores fault codes (DTCs) and lights the malfunction indicator lamp (MIL).
Lubrication system controlVariable-displacement oil pump control; oil pressure and level monitoring.
Throttle controlElectronic throttle (drive-by-wire): converts pedal position into a throttle angle and also serves cruise control, TCS and ESP torque requests.

1.4 Chassis Electronics

The chassis system contains many sub-systems that monitor vehicle parameters and act on them:

  • ABS (Anti-lock Braking System): stops the wheels from locking when braking, so the car can still be steered (Chapter 3).
  • TCS (Traction Control System): stops the driven wheels from spinning when accelerating (Chapter 5).
  • EBD (Electronic Brake-force Distribution): shares brake force between the front and rear axles (and left/right) according to the load on each, so the rear wheels do not lock first. It uses the ABS hardware.
  • ESP (Electronic Stability Program): corrects understeer and oversteer by braking individual wheels (Chapter 6).
  • PA (Parking Assistance): ultrasonic sensors and cameras help the driver park, or park the car automatically.

1.4.1 Engine electronics vs chassis electronics

AspectEngine electronicsChassis electronics
What it controlsThe power source: combustion, air–fuel mixture, ignition, emissions and engine auxiliariesThe motion of the vehicle on the road: braking, traction, stability, steering, suspension
Main goalTorque and power, fuel economy, low emissions, engine protectionSafety, stability, steerability and ride comfort
Typical systemsEngine ECU: fuel injection, ignition timing, throttle (drive-by-wire), turbo boost, EGR, lambda control, cooling, OBDABS, TCS, EBD, ESP, electric power steering, active suspension, parking assistance
Key sensorsCrankshaft and camshaft position, air-mass/MAP, throttle position, coolant temperature, oxygen (lambda), knockWheel speed, steering angle, yaw rate, lateral acceleration, brake pressure, ride height
ActuatorsInjectors, ignition coils, throttle motor, wastegate, EGR valveHydraulic modulator valves and pump, steering motor, adjustable dampers
Timing demandHard real time, synchronised to crank angle (microsecond precision at high rpm)Real time in milliseconds (ABS cycles 4–10 times per second per wheel)
Where it actsInside the powertrain, before the wheelsAt the wheels and body; it requests engine torque changes over CAN when needed (TCS, ESP)

1.5 Automotive Safety: Active and Passive

AspectActive safetyPassive safety
DefinitionFeatures that help avoid an accidentFeatures that reduce the effect (injury) of an accident once it happens
ActsBefore the crash (continuously while driving)During and after the crash
ExamplesClear warning symbols, ABS, TPMS (tyre-pressure monitoring), intelligent speed adaptation, traction control, ESP, lane assist, autonomous emergency brakingPassenger safety cell (rigid cabin with crumple zones), seat belts and pretensioners, airbags, correctly positioned fuel tank, collapsible steering column, head restraints
Sensors usedWheel speed, yaw rate, radar, camera, tyre pressureCrash accelerometers, seat occupancy, belt buckle switches

1.6 Driver Assistance Systems

  • Lane assist: a camera finds the lane markings and warns the driver, or steers gently, when the car drifts out of its lane.
  • Speed assist: recognises speed-limit signs and warns the driver or limits the car's speed.
  • Blind-spot detection: rear radar sensors warn of a vehicle in the blind spot when changing lanes.
  • Park assist: ultrasonic sensors and cameras guide or perform the parking manoeuvre.
  • Adaptive cruise control (ACC): radar keeps a set time gap to the car in front (see §4.7).
  • Pre-collision assist: detects an imminent collision, warns the driver, pre-fills the brakes and brakes automatically if needed.

1.6.1 Evolution of automotive electronics (useful for “significance over the years”)

PeriodMilestoneEffect on the vehicle
1960s–70sSolid-state voltage regulators, transistorised and electronic ignitionReliable ignition, less maintenance
Late 1970sMicroprocessor engine control; first production 4-wheel electronic ABS (Bosch, 1978)Lower emissions and fuel use; steerable emergency braking
1980sElectronic fuel injection (EFI) with lambda control; TCS; electronic transmission controlCatalytic converters became workable; better driveability
1990sCAN bus in production cars (1991); airbags become standard; OBD-II (1996); ESP (1995)Networked ECUs, less wiring, large safety gains
2000sDrive-by-wire throttle, EPS, hybrid vehicles (Prius 1997/2000), TPMS, ACCSoftware-defined functions, higher efficiency
2010s–nowMass-market EVs, ADAS (AEB, lane keeping), automotive Ethernet, over-the-air updates, Level 2+ automationCar as a “computer on wheels”; 70–150 ECUs per vehicle

1.7 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q5(a)Define Autotronics. Explain the significance of electronics for improving the overall performance of automotive vehicle over the years.10Topic: autotronics

Definition. Autotronics (Automotive + Electronics) is the field of electronic systems used in vehicles: engine management, ignition, transmission control, braking and stability control, safety, comfort, radio, telematics and in-car entertainment. These are automotive embedded systems, meaning microcontroller-based ECUs with sensors and actuators, linked by in-vehicle networks such as CAN and LIN.

Significance of electronics in improving vehicle performance:

  1. Engine performance and fuel economy: Carburettors and mechanical distributors were replaced by electronic fuel injection and mapped ignition. The ECU meters fuel accurately for every cycle and sets the best spark advance using knock control. The result is more power per litre, easier cold starts and lower fuel consumption.
  2. Emission reduction: Closed-loop lambda control holds the air–fuel ratio at stoichiometric, which lets the three-way catalytic converter remove more than 90% of CO, HC and NOₓ. OBD watches emission-related parts all the time. Without electronics, modern emission norms (Euro 6 etc.) could not be met.
  3. Safety: ABS keeps the car steerable in panic braking. TCS prevents wheel spin. ESP prevents skidding. Airbags and belt pretensioners fire within milliseconds of a crash. ADAS (lane assist, AEB) prevents many accidents altogether. ESP alone is estimated to have prevented a large share of single-vehicle loss-of-control accidents.
  4. Transmission and driveability: Electronically controlled automatic gearboxes, DCTs and CVTs shift smoothly at the ideal moments, improving both performance and economy.
  5. Comfort and convenience: Climate control, power steering (EPS), cruise control, keyless entry and electronically adjusted suspension.
  6. Diagnostics and maintenance: Fault codes stored in the ECU (OBD) allow quick, accurate fault finding and reduce downtime.
  7. Networking and integration: CAN lets ECUs share sensor data, so one wheel-speed sensor serves ABS, TCS, ESP, the speedometer and the navigation system. This reduces wiring weight and cost and makes functions such as ESP possible, since ESP needs coordinated engine and brake control.
  8. Electrification and autonomy: Hybrid and electric vehicles (battery management, motor inverters, regenerative braking) and self-driving functions depend entirely on power electronics and computing.

Conclusion: Over the years electronics has changed the car from a mainly mechanical machine into a mechatronic system. The share of E/E in vehicle value has risen from a few percent to about a third or more, and most innovation in performance, efficiency, emissions and safety now comes from electronics and software.

Source lectureKMS · L1–L2 – Intro & Autotronics (AVT_L1-L2_MT.pdf, pp. 4–9)
2022 · Q5(b) | 2023 · Q7(b)Classify automotive safety devices with necessary examples.10 / 08Topic: safety devices

Automotive safety devices are classified into two groups according to when they act relative to an accident:

1. Active safety devices help the driver avoid an accident by keeping the vehicle controllable and warning of danger:

  • Anti-lock braking system: stops the wheels locking, so the car can still be steered while braking hard.
  • Traction control: stops wheel spin when accelerating on slippery roads.
  • Tyre-pressure monitoring system (TPMS): warns of under-inflation, which would otherwise cause poor handling, longer braking distances or a blow-out.
  • Intelligent speed adaptation: warns the driver of, or enforces, the local speed limit.
  • Legibility of warning symbols: clear warning lamps and messages tell the driver about faults immediately.

2. Passive safety devices reduce the consequences of an accident once it cannot be avoided:

  • Passenger safety cell: a rigid cabin surrounded by crumple zones that absorb crash energy.
  • Seat belts: hold the occupants in their seats. Pretensioners tighten the belt in the first milliseconds of a crash.
  • Air bags: inflate within about 30 ms to cushion the head and chest.
  • Correctly positioned fuel tank: placed inside the protected area to prevent fuel leaks and fire after a crash.

Modern cars also add integrated safety, where active sensors trigger passive measures early. For example, pre-crash systems tighten the belts and close the windows when radar detects that a crash cannot be avoided.

Source lectureKMS · L1–L2 – Intro & Autotronics (AVT_L1-L2_MT.pdf, pp. 12–13)
2024 · Q5(a)Define autotronics. How has the integration of autotronics driven the evolution of modern automobile systems and redefined the technological trajectory of the automotive industry?10Topic: autotronics

Definition. Autotronics (Automotive + Electronics) covers the electronic systems used in vehicles for engine management, ignition, transmission, chassis control, safety, comfort, infotainment and telematics. These systems are built as distributed automotive embedded systems (ECUs, sensors, actuators and networks).

How autotronics drove the evolution of automobile systems:

  1. From mechanical to electronic control: Carburettors became electronic fuel injection, the contact-breaker ignition became mapped electronic ignition, and mechanical throttle linkages became drive-by-wire. Control moved from fixed mechanical settings to software that adapts to every operating condition.
  2. New functions that mechanics alone could not provide: ABS, TCS and ESP need wheel-by-wheel brake pressure modulation many times a second, decided by a microcontroller. Airbags need crash detection within milliseconds.
  3. From stand-alone ECUs to networked systems: CAN, LIN, FlexRay, MOST and now automotive Ethernet let 70–150 ECUs share data. Features became cross-domain: ESP combines braking and engine control, and ACC combines radar, engine and brakes.
  4. Electrification: Power electronics, battery management and motor control made hybrids and electric vehicles possible. Regenerative braking blends friction and electric braking under ECU control.
  5. Driver assistance and autonomy: Sensors (camera, radar, LiDAR) plus powerful processors enabled ADAS and then automated driving, which is autotronics at its most advanced.
  6. Connectivity and the software-defined vehicle: telematics, infotainment, over-the-air software updates and centralised domain/zonal computers.

How autotronics redefined the industry's technological trajectory:

  • Value has shifted from mechanical hardware to electronics and software. Semiconductor, software and sensor companies are now key automotive suppliers.
  • Development now needs mechatronic and software engineering skills: model-based design, hardware-in-the-loop testing, AUTOSAR and functional safety (ISO 26262).
  • Competition now turns on efficiency (EVs), safety ratings (ADAS) and user experience (infotainment, OTA updates) more than on engine displacement.
  • Regulation depends on electronics: emission norms need OBD, and many markets now require ABS and ESC.

Conclusion: Autotronics has turned the automobile from a mechanical machine into an intelligent, networked, electrified mechatronic system. It sets the industry's path toward electric, connected, automated and software-defined vehicles.

Source lectureKMS · L1–L2 – Intro & Autotronics (AVT_L1-L2_MT.pdf, pp. 4–9) — Industry-evolution discussion only implied (p. 5 figure)
2023 · Q5(a)What is meant by advanced vehicle technology? Explain the relationship of the term “Autotronics” with advanced vehicle technology.10Topic: AVT · autotronics

Advanced Vehicle Technology (AVT) is the application of innovative, cutting-edge technologies to the design and development of vehicles, to improve their performance, safety, efficiency and sustainability (lecture). Heisler describes it as vehicles that use new technologies to improve fuel efficiency, reduce emissions, enhance safety and increase comfort and convenience. Rajamani describes it as the study of advanced propulsion, vehicle dynamics and control, and vehicle safety systems, to improve performance while reducing environmental impact (§1.1).

Autotronics (Automotive + Electronics) is the field of electronic systems used in vehicles: engine management, ignition, transmission, braking and stability control, safety, infotainment and telematics. These are distributed embedded systems of ECUs, sensors and actuators linked by networks such as CAN and LIN (§1.2).

Relationship. AVT is the goal (a better vehicle); autotronics is the main means of reaching it. Almost every AVT feature is an autotronic system:

AVT objectiveAutotronic system that delivers it
Performance and fuel efficiencyEngine ECU: electronic fuel injection, ignition timing, turbo-boost and throttle control; electronic transmission control
Low emissionsClosed-loop lambda control, EGR, catalyst management, on-board diagnostics (OBD)
SafetyABS, TCS, ESP, EBD (active); airbag and belt-pretensioner control units (passive)
Comfort and convenienceCruise control, automatic climate control, power steering, infotainment
Advanced propulsionHybrid and electric drives: inverters, motor controllers, battery management systems, regenerative braking
Driver assistance and autonomyRadar, camera and LiDAR processing; ADAS ECUs; high-speed networks (CAN FD, automotive Ethernet)

So the two grow together: new AVT goals (stricter emission rules, safety ratings, electrification, automation) create demand for more electronics, and cheaper, faster electronics make new AVT features possible. The lecture's Bosch figure shows the share of electrics/electronics in a car's value rising from a few percent to about a third or more, and today's cars carry 70–150 ECUs. In short, autotronics is the backbone of advanced vehicle technology.

Source lectureKMS · L1–L2 – Intro & Autotronics (AVT_L1-L2_MT.pdf, pp. 4–7)
2023 · Q5(b)Draw distinction between engine electronics and chassis electronics. Why air bags are considered as passive safety device?10Topic: engine vs chassis electronics · airbags

Engine vs chassis electronics: write the table of §1.4.1. In short, engine electronics controls the power source (fuel injection, ignition, throttle, turbo, emissions, cooling, OBD) to give torque, economy and low emissions, under hard crank-angle-synchronised real-time demands. Chassis electronics controls how the vehicle moves on the road (ABS, TCS, EBD, ESP, power steering, parking assistance) to give safety, stability and comfort, using wheel-speed, steering-angle and yaw-rate sensors and the brake modulator. Chassis systems ask the engine ECU for torque changes over CAN, so the two domains cooperate.

Why airbags are passive safety devices. Active safety features help to avoid an accident (ABS, TCS, ESP, TPMS). Passive safety features do nothing to prevent the crash; they reduce the effect of an accident once it happens (§1.5). An airbag acts only during the collision:

  1. Crash sensors (accelerometers in the airbag control unit, plus satellite sensors in the front and sides) measure the vehicle's deceleration.
  2. If the deceleration pattern exceeds the deployment threshold (a frontal impact equal to hitting a wall at roughly 20–25 km/h), the control unit fires the igniter within about 10–20 ms.
  3. A gas generator inflates the nylon bag in about 30 ms, between the occupant and the steering wheel, dashboard or door.
  4. The bag cushions the occupant, spreads the load over a large area and then vents through holes, so the occupant is not thrown back.

It cannot help the driver avoid the crash. It only lowers injury once the crash is under way, together with the seat belt (hence the name SRS, Supplementary Restraint System). That is exactly the definition of a passive safety device.

Source lectureKMS · L1–L2 – Intro & Autotronics (AVT_L1-L2_MT.pdf, pp. 7–9, 12–13) — Airbag deployment sequence not in slides; see §1.5

2. Electronic Control Unit (ECU) & In-Vehicle Networks ★★★

2.1 Definition and Role

Definition
An Electronic Control Unit (ECU), also called an Electronic Control Module (ECM), is an embedded system in automotive electronics that controls one or more of the electrical systems or subsystems in a car or other motor vehicle. The control unit receives electrical signals from sensors, evaluates them, and calculates the triggering signals for the actuators. The control program (the software) is stored in a special memory and executed by a microcontroller. The control unit and its components are called the hardware.

Digital technology gives a very wide range of options for open-loop and closed-loop control of automotive systems. The same hardware can do very different jobs depending on its software, and the software can be recalibrated for different engines or vehicle models without changing the hardware. A modern car contains many ECUs: engine (ECM), transmission (TCU), brake/ABS-ESP, airbag (ACU), body control module (BCM), instrument cluster, infotainment, battery management (in EVs) and others.

2.2 Operating Conditions

An ECU works in one of the harshest environments for electronics. It must operate reliably under:

  • Extreme ambient temperatures: from −40 °C up to +60 … +125 °C in normal vehicle operation (the higher values apply near the engine).
  • Extreme temperature changes: thermal cycling stresses solder joints.
  • Exposure to fluids such as oil and fuel.
  • Moisture and condensation.
  • Mechanical stress such as engine vibration and shock.
  • Supply voltage variations: the ECU must work when cranking with a weak battery (e.g. a cold start, when the voltage can fall to about 6 V) and with high charging voltages and transients (load dump) from the vehicle electrical system.
  • Electromagnetic interference from ignition, motors and radio (EMC requirements).

2.3 Components of an ECU

2.3.1 Input sensors

Input sensors measure physical quantities such as engine speed, vehicle speed, temperature, pressure and position, and turn them into electrical signals. The ECU uses this data to decide how to control the vehicle's systems. Sensor signals come in three kinds: analog (e.g. a coolant NTC thermistor voltage), digital/switching (e.g. a brake-light switch) and pulse-shaped (e.g. crankshaft or wheel-speed sensors, whose frequency carries the information). Examples: crankshaft position sensor, coolant temperature sensor, manifold absolute pressure sensor, throttle position sensor, oxygen sensor, knock sensor.

Crankshaft position sensor: how the ECU measures speed (lecture figure)
An inductive or Hall-effect sensor faces a toothed trigger wheel on the crankshaft, typically a 60−2 wheel with a gap marking top dead centre. Each passing tooth produces one pulse, and signal conditioning squares this into a digital signal. Inside the microcontroller a free-running timer/counter is read at every tooth edge: TnT_nTn​ is the counter status at tooth nnn and Tn+1T_{n+1}Tn+1​ is the status at tooth n+1n+1n+1. The difference gives the time the crankshaft took to turn through one tooth angle: Δt=Tn+1−Tnfcounter,nengine [rpm]=(tooth angle in ∘)/360∘Δt×60\Delta t=\frac{T_{n+1}-T_n}{f_{\text{counter}}},\qquad n_{\text{engine}}\ [\text{rpm}]=\frac{(\text{tooth angle in }^\circ)/360^\circ}{\Delta t}\times60Δt=fcounter​Tn+1​−Tn​​,nengine​ [rpm]=Δt(tooth angle in ∘)/360∘​×60 The missing-tooth gap produces an unusually long Δt, which gives the ECU the absolute crank position (TDC) needed to time injection and ignition.

2.3.2 Output actuators

Output actuators turn the ECU's electrical commands into physical action: fuel injectors (injection system), ignition coils (ignition system), the electronic throttle motor, solenoid valves in the transmission or ABS modulator, and relays, pumps and fans. They are driven by power output stages (low-side/high-side MOSFET drivers, H-bridges, PWM) inside the ECU, which the microcontroller's low-power pins cannot drive directly.

2.3.3 Microcontroller

The microcontroller is the brain of the ECU. It runs the control software, reads the sensors through its ADCs, timers and digital inputs, carries out the control algorithms (maps, PID, observers), and writes the actuator commands. Automotive MCUs are qualified for the temperature range and include functional-safety features such as lock-step cores, ECC memory and watchdogs. The lecture example is the Renesas RH850 family: 32-bit automotive MCUs offering high performance with very low power consumption, over a wide and scalable range, with the functional-safety and embedded-security features needed by new automotive applications. (Other examples: Infineon AURIX TC3xx, NXP S32K, ST SPC5.)

2.3.4 Communication interfaces

Modern ECUs include communication interfaces such as CAN (Controller Area Network) and LIN (Local Interconnect Network) to exchange data with other ECUs. The lecture examples are the TJA1145 CAN transceiver (named on the slide as Texas Instruments; the TJA1145 part number is NXP's) and the NXP SJA1105 automotive Ethernet switch. The CAN controller is usually built into the MCU. The external transceiver converts its logic-level signals into the differential bus voltages. See §2.5 for details.

2.3.5 Memory

  • Flash / ROM: holds the program code and the calibration data (characteristic maps) permanently.
  • EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM): holds data that must survive power-off but may change, such as adaptation values, fault codes (DTCs), the odometer and immobiliser codes.
  • RAM: holds variables and intermediate results while running. Its contents are lost at power-off.

Lecture example: the NXP S32K microcontroller family, which includes Flash and EEPROM memory.

2.3.6 Power supply

The ECU needs a stable power supply, provided by the vehicle battery (12 V, or 24 V in trucks) or an external source. An internal regulator turns the fluctuating battery voltage (roughly 6–16 V, with transients) into clean 5 V or 3.3 V rails. It includes reverse-polarity protection, transient and load-dump suppression, and a low-voltage reset.

2.4 In-Vehicle Network Classes (lecture table)

ClassTransfer rateApplicationsRepresentative
ALow (up to 10 kbit/s)Actuator and sensor networkingLIN
BAverage (up to 125 kbit/s)Complex mechanisms for error handling; control-unit networking in comfort functionsLow-speed CAN
CHigh (up to 1 Mbit/s)Real-time requirements; control-unit networking in drive and running-gear functionsHigh-speed CAN
C+Extremely high (up to 10 Mbit/s)Real-time, control-unit networking in drive and running-gear functions (safety-critical, x-by-wire)FlexRay
DExtremely high (> 10 Mbit/s)Control-unit networking in telematics and multimediaMOST (now automotive Ethernet)

Lecture examples of networked operation. Turn signalling: the steering-column switch sends a message on the comfort CAN. The body control unit flashes the indicator lamps, and a gateway passes the status to the instrument-cluster CAN to light the indicator symbol and click the relay sound. Windshield-wiper operation: the wiper stalk's command travels over comfort CAN to the body control unit, which then drives the wiper motor over a LIN sub-bus. This shows the typical CAN backbone with LIN branches.

2.5 Controller Area Network (CAN) in Depth

What CAN is
CAN is a serial, multi-master, message-based bus developed by Bosch (1983, first used in production in 1991) so that ECUs can communicate without a host computer. Every ECU (node) connects to the same two-wire twisted pair (CAN_H and CAN_L). Messages are not addressed to a node. Each message carries an identifier (ID) that describes its content (e.g. “engine speed”) and also sets its priority. Every node receives every message and uses acceptance filters to keep the ones it needs.

2.5.1 How CAN makes communication among ECUs possible

  1. Physical layer (differential signalling): Each bit is sent as the voltage difference between CAN_H and CAN_L. Noise induced on the twisted pair affects both wires equally (common mode) and cancels out, so CAN is very robust against the electrical noise in a car. A dominant bit (logical 0) drives the lines apart. A recessive bit (logical 1) lets them float to the same level. If any node sends a dominant bit, the bus is dominant (wired-AND).
  2. Broadcast and content addressing: A sender puts a message such as “engine speed = 2150 rpm, ID 0x0C0” on the bus. All ECUs receive it, and those that need it (TCU, cluster, ESP) accept it. Nodes can be added without changing the others.
  3. Bus access by non-destructive bitwise arbitration (CSMA/CR): A node may start sending when the bus is idle. If two nodes start together, each sends its ID bit by bit and reads the bus back. A node that sends recessive (1) but reads dominant (0) knows a higher-priority message is on the bus. It stops sending and becomes a receiver. The message with the lowest ID wins and goes through undisturbed, with no time lost. Important messages (e.g. brake data) therefore always get through first.
  4. Frame structure: Every message is packed into a standard frame (table below) with up to 8 data bytes (64 bytes in CAN FD).
  5. Error detection and confinement: CRC check, bit monitoring, bit stuffing, frame check and acknowledgement. A node that detects an error sends an error frame, and the message is automatically resent. Error counters switch a faulty node to “error passive” and then “bus off”, so one broken ECU cannot block the network.
  6. Gateways connect several CAN buses running at different speeds (powertrain CAN at 500 kbit/s, comfort CAN at 100–125 kbit/s) and LIN sub-buses. They pass on only the messages that each network needs.
Field (standard frame, CAN 2.0A)BitsPurpose
SOF (Start of Frame)1Dominant bit that synchronises all nodes
Identifier11 (29 in extended 2.0B)Message content and priority (lower = higher priority)
RTR1Data frame (dominant) or remote request (recessive)
Control (IDE, r0, DLC)6Identifier format and Data Length Code (0–8 bytes)
Data0–64Payload (0–8 bytes)
CRC + delimiter15 + 1Cyclic redundancy check for error detection
ACK slot + delimiter1 + 1Any receiver that got the frame correctly writes a dominant bit
EOF7End of frame (recessive)
IFS (interframe space)3Minimum gap before the next frame
Frame length and time
Bits without stuffing = 1 + 11 + 1 + 6 + 8·DLC + 16 + 2 + 7 = 44 + 8·DLC (plus 3 IFS bits). After every 5 identical bits a stuff bit is inserted. In the worst case this adds ⌊(34 + 8·DLC − 1)/4⌋ bits. tframe=(number of bits)×tbit,tbit=1bit ratet_{\text{frame}}=(\text{number of bits})\times t_{\text{bit}},\qquad t_{\text{bit}}=\frac{1}{\text{bit rate}}tframe​=(number of bits)×tbit​,tbit​=bit rate1​

2.5.2 Why CAN is preferred in modern vehicles

AdvantageExplanation
Less wiring, weight and costOne twisted pair replaces hundreds of point-to-point wires. Sensor data is shared (one wheel-speed signal serves ABS, ESP, TCS, speedometer and navigation).
Real-time priorityDeterministic, non-destructive arbitration: safety-critical messages with low IDs always win with bounded delay.
High reliabilityDifferential signalling rejects noise. Five error-detection mechanisms, automatic retransmission and fault confinement give a very low residual error rate.
Multi-master, flexibleNo central master that could fail. ECUs can be added or removed without redesigning the network.
Standardised and cheapISO 11898. CAN controllers are built into almost every automotive MCU, and transceivers are inexpensive.
DiagnosticsOBD-II/UDS diagnostics run over CAN, so one connector gives access to all ECUs.
Proven and scalableDecades of field use. CAN FD raises the data rate and payload for newer needs.

N2.2 CAN frame time and bus load

A high-speed CAN runs at 500 kbit/s. An engine ECU sends one standard frame with 8 data bytes every 10 ms. Find (a) the frame time without stuffing, (b) the worst-case frame time, (c) the bus load from this message.

Given Data
Bit rate 500 kbit/s  |  standard (11-bit ID) frame, DLC = 8  |  period 10 ms

[KEY IDENTITY]Frame bits =44+8⋅=44+8\cdot=44+8⋅DLC; only the 34 + 8·DLC bits from SOF to the CRC can be stuffed.

[INTUITION]Bus load = busy time ÷ message period.

N2.3 CAN arbitration

The ESP ECU (ID 0x065) and the instrument cluster (ID 0x06A) start sending at the same moment. Which message wins?

Given Data
ESP ID = 0x065  |  cluster ID = 0x06A  |  both start together
Step 1: Binary IDs (11 bit). 0x065 = 000 0110 0101; 0x06A = 000 0110 1010.
Step 2: Bit-by-bit. The first 7 bits (0000110) are identical. At bit 8 the ESP node sends 0 (dominant) and the cluster sends 1 (recessive). The bus shows dominant, so the cluster reads back a bit that differs from what it sent and withdraws.
Result: ESP message (0x065) wins. The lower ID has the higher priority. The cluster retries automatically as soon as the bus is idle.
[KEY IDENTITY]Dominant 0 overwrites recessive 1 on the bus (wired-AND).

[INTUITION]Arbitration is non-destructive: the winning frame is not delayed at all.

PointSensorActuator

2.8 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q5(c)What is Electronic Control Unit (ECU)? What are the components of ECU? Briefly explain the functionality of each component.15Topic: ECU components

ECU. An Electronic Control Unit (or Electronic Control Module) is an embedded system in automotive electronics that controls one or more of the electrical systems or subsystems of a vehicle. It receives electrical signals from sensors, evaluates them using a control program stored in memory and executed by a microcontroller, and calculates the triggering signals for the actuators. Examples: the engine ECU, ABS/ESP ECU, transmission control unit and airbag control unit.

Draw Fig. 2.1 (sensors → input conditioning → microcontroller ↔ memory → output stages → actuators, with power supply and CAN interface).

Components and their functions:

  1. Input sensors: measure parameters such as engine speed, vehicle speed, temperature and pressure, and convert them into electrical signals that the ECU uses for its decisions. Examples: the crankshaft position sensor (engine speed and TDC), the coolant temperature sensor (warm-up enrichment, fan control). The ECU's input circuits filter, amplify and protect these signals and convert analog values to digital (ADC).
  2. Microcontroller: the brain of the ECU. It runs the control program, processes the sensor data using maps and control algorithms, and computes the output commands in real time (e.g. injection duration and spark advance for every cylinder). Example: the Renesas RH850 32-bit automotive MCU, with high performance, low power and functional-safety and security features.
  3. Memory: ROM/Flash holds the program and calibration maps permanently. EEPROM holds changing data that must survive power-off (fault codes, adaptive values). RAM holds working variables. Example: the NXP S32K family, with built-in Flash and EEPROM.
  4. Output actuators (and output drivers): the ECU's power stages drive actuators that act on the vehicle: fuel injectors, ignition coils, throttle motor, transmission solenoids.
  5. Communication interfaces: CAN or LIN controllers and transceivers let the ECU exchange data with other ECUs and with diagnostic testers (OBD). Examples: the TJA1145 CAN transceiver and the NXP SJA1105 automotive Ethernet switch.
  6. Power supply: supplies stable regulated voltage (5 V/3.3 V) from the vehicle battery. It must cope with a weak battery during a cold start and with high charging voltages and transients.

How it works together: sensor → input conditioning → MCU computes using its program and memory → output drivers → actuator, with data shared over CAN. The whole unit must work from −40 °C to +125 °C and withstand vibration, moisture, oil and fuel.

Source lectureKMS · L3 – Electronic Control Unit (AVT_20L3.pptx, slides 6–16)
2024 · Q5(b)Explain the significance of an Electronic Control Unit (ECU) in automobiles. Discuss its major hardware components and their roles.15Topic: ECU hardware

Significance of the ECU:

  1. Precise real-time control: The ECU adjusts fuel injection, ignition timing and throttle for every engine cycle according to speed, load and temperature. A fixed mechanical system cannot do this. The result is more power, better economy and smoother running.
  2. Emission compliance: Closed-loop lambda control, EGR and catalyst management, plus on-board diagnostics, are only possible with an ECU.
  3. Safety functions: ABS, TCS, ESP and airbags depend on ECUs that sense and react within milliseconds.
  4. Adaptability: The same hardware can be recalibrated or reprogrammed (even over the air) for different models, markets and fuel qualities. Adaptive learning compensates for component ageing.
  5. Diagnostics: The ECU detects faults, stores trouble codes and warns the driver, which makes servicing faster.
  6. Integration: Through CAN, ECUs share information and coordinate functions (e.g. TCS asking the engine ECU to cut torque, or the TCU requesting torque reduction during a gear shift).
  7. Comfort and efficiency: automatic climate control, cruise control, start-stop and, in EVs, battery and motor management.

Major hardware components and roles (draw Fig. 2.1):

ComponentRole
Input sensors and input circuitsSense engine speed, temperature, pressure, position etc. Input circuits filter, amplify, protect and digitise (ADC) the signals and shape pulses.
Microcontroller (CPU)Runs the control software, evaluates the inputs, computes outputs in real time and manages diagnostics (e.g. Renesas RH850).
MemoryFlash/ROM: program and calibration maps. EEPROM: fault codes and learned values. RAM: runtime data (e.g. NXP S32K with Flash and EEPROM).
Output stages and actuatorsPower drivers switch injectors, ignition coils, valves and motors.
Communication interfaceCAN/LIN/Ethernet controllers and transceivers for data exchange and diagnostics (e.g. TJA1145 CAN transceiver).
Power supplyRegulates battery voltage to stable logic levels and protects against reverse polarity, load dump and cranking dips.
Housing and connectorsProtect the electronics from −40 to +125 °C, moisture, oil, fuel and vibration.
Source lectureKMS · L3 – Electronic Control Unit (AVT_20L3.pptx, slides 4–16)
2024 · Q5(c)Discuss how Controller Area Network (CAN) facilitates communication among ECUs. Why is CAN preferred in modern vehicles?10Topic: CAN bus

CAN is a serial, multi-master, message-based bus (ISO 11898) that connects all ECUs over one twisted pair (CAN_H, CAN_L), terminated with 120 Ω at both ends (draw Fig. 2.2).

How it makes communication possible:

  1. Differential two-wire signalling: a dominant bit (0) makes CAN_H ≈ 3.5 V and CAN_L ≈ 1.5 V. A recessive bit (1) leaves both at ≈ 2.5 V. Noise affects both wires equally and cancels out.
  2. Broadcast, content-based messages: each frame carries an 11-bit (or 29-bit) identifier describing its content, such as “wheel speeds”. All ECUs receive every frame and accept the ones they need, so one sensor's data serves many ECUs.
  3. Arbitration: any node may start sending when the bus is idle. When several start at once, bitwise arbitration on the identifier lets the message with the lowest ID (highest priority) continue. The others back off and retry, and no data is lost (CSMA/CR).
  4. Frame: SOF, ID, RTR, control (DLC), 0–8 data bytes, CRC, ACK and EOF. Receivers acknowledge correct frames.
  5. Error handling: CRC, bit monitoring, stuffing, form and ACK checks. Errors trigger an error frame and automatic retransmission. Faulty nodes are isolated (bus-off).
  6. Gateways link powertrain CAN (500 kbit/s), comfort CAN (125 kbit/s) and LIN sub-networks. Example: a turn-signal command travels over comfort CAN, and the gateway forwards the status to the instrument-cluster CAN.

Why CAN is preferred: (i) much less wiring, weight and cost; (ii) real-time, priority-based deterministic access; (iii) high noise immunity and reliability with strong error detection; (iv) multi-master with no single point of failure, and easy to extend; (v) standardised, inexpensive and built into most automotive MCUs; (vi) supports on-board diagnostics through one port; (vii) proven over decades, with CAN FD for higher bandwidth.

Source lectureKMS · L3 – Electronic Control Unit (AVT_20L3.pptx, slides 12–14) — CAN frame, arbitration and bus wiring not in slides
2023 · Q5(c)What is the significance of using communication interfaces in electronic control unit (ECU)? Discuss about different types of communication interfaces used in ECUs.15Topic: ECU communication interfaces

A communication interface is the part of an ECU (protocol controller inside the microcontroller plus a bus transceiver) that lets it exchange data with other ECUs, sensors and testers over an in-vehicle network (§2.3.4).

Significance:

  1. Distributed functions need shared data. A modern car has 70–150 ECUs. Many functions use several of them: TCS and ESP ask the engine ECU to cut torque; the transmission ECU asks for torque reduction during a shift; ACC/cruise control works with ESP.
  2. Sensor sharing. One wheel-speed signal is used by ABS, ESP, the speedometer, navigation and the transmission. It is measured once and broadcast, so no sensor is duplicated.
  3. Less wiring. A two-wire bus replaces hundreds of point-to-point wires. This saves weight, cost and connectors, and improves reliability.
  4. Real-time and safety. Priority-based arbitration (CAN) or time-triggered scheduling (FlexRay) delivers safety-critical messages on time. CRC, acknowledgement and error confinement detect faults.
  5. Diagnostics and software updates. Fault codes are read and software is flashed through the OBD port and gateway; many cars now update over the air.
  6. Flexibility. Optional equipment is added by connecting another node, without rewiring the car.

Types of communication interfaces (by SAE class, §2.4):

InterfaceClass / speedPrincipleTypical use
LINA, ≤ 20 kbit/sSingle wire, one master and up to 16 slaves; cheap UART-basedWindow lifters, mirrors, wipers, seat motors, rain sensor
Low-speed CANB, ≤ 125 kbit/sFault-tolerant two-wire CANComfort and body electronics
High-speed CAN / CAN FDC, ≤ 1 Mbit/s (FD up to 5–8 Mbit/s)Multi-master, twisted pair, non-destructive bitwise arbitration, CRCEngine, transmission, ABS/ESP, airbag (powertrain and chassis)
FlexRayC+, 10 Mbit/sTime-triggered (TDMA), deterministic, two redundant channelsSafety-critical x-by-wire, active suspension
MOSTD, 25–150 Mbit/sOptical ringAudio, video, infotainment
Automotive EthernetD, 100 Mbit/s – 10 Gbit/sSwitched point-to-point links (e.g. NXP SJA1105 switch, lecture)Cameras, ADAS, backbone, over-the-air updates
Diagnostic interfaceOBD-II (CAN, older K-line)Tester connects through the OBD port and gatewayReading fault codes, flashing software

Inside the ECU, the protocol controller (e.g. the CAN controller in the microcontroller) builds and checks the frames, and the transceiver (e.g. the TJA1145 CAN transceiver named in the lecture) converts logic levels into the differential bus voltages. A gateway ECU joins the different buses and passes messages between them (Figure 2.3). CAN is described in detail in §2.5.

Source lectureKMS · L3 – Electronic Control Unit (AVT_20L3.pptx, slides 7, 12–14) — Significance list and other network types from §2.4–2.5
2023 · Q6(a)Discuss about the operation of crankshaft position sensor as an input sensor in ECUs.10Topic: crankshaft position sensor

Purpose. The crankshaft position sensor (CKP) is the most important input of the engine ECU. It gives the engine speed and the angular position of the crankshaft. The ECU needs both to time fuel injection and ignition for each cylinder, to limit engine speed and to detect misfires. Without the CKP signal the engine will not start.

Construction. A toothed trigger (reluctor) wheel is fixed to the crankshaft or flywheel, usually with 60 − 2 teeth: 58 teeth with a gap of two missing teeth that marks a reference position (e.g. TDC of cylinder 1). The sensor faces the teeth with a small air gap. There are two types:

  • Inductive (magnetic) sensor: a permanent magnet with a soft-iron pole piece and a coil. Each passing tooth changes the magnetic flux, which induces an AC voltage in the coil. Its frequency and amplitude rise with speed, so a minimum speed is needed.
  • Hall-effect sensor: a Hall element with built-in electronics gives a digital square wave whose amplitude does not depend on speed, so it works even at very low speed.

Operation as an ECU input (lecture figure, §2.3.1):

  1. Signal conditioning: the analog sensor voltage is filtered and squared by a comparator (Schmitt trigger) into clean digital pulses, one per tooth.
  2. Time measurement: a free-running timer/counter in the microcontroller is captured at every tooth edge. TnT_nTn​ and Tn+1T_{n+1}Tn+1​ are the counter values at two successive teeth.
  3. Speed calculation: Δt=(Tn+1−Tn)/fcounter\Delta t=(T_{n+1}-T_n)/f_{\text{counter}}Δt=(Tn+1​−Tn​)/fcounter​ is the time for one tooth pitch (6° on a 60-tooth wheel), so n=6∘/360∘Δt×60n=\dfrac{6^\circ/360^\circ}{\Delta t}\times60n=Δt6∘/360∘​×60 rpm. Example N2.1: 500 µs per tooth gives 2000 rpm.
  4. Position (reference mark): at the missing-tooth gap Δt\Delta tΔt is about three times longer. The ECU recognises it as the reference mark and from then on counts teeth to know the exact crank angle.
  5. Cylinder identification: the crankshaft turns twice per cycle in a four-stroke engine, so the ECU combines the CKP signal with the camshaft sensor to know which cylinder is on its compression stroke.
  6. Use of the result: the ECU schedules injector opening and spark timing at the correct crank angle, and detects misfires from small speed drops between firing pulses.
Source lectureKMS · L3 – Electronic Control Unit (AVT_20L3.pptx, slides 8–9) — Sensor principle and speed calculation not in slides; see §2.3.1

3. Anti-lock Braking System (ABS) ★★★

3.1 Definition and Objective

Definition
An anti-lock braking system (ABS) is an anti-skid safety braking system used on aircraft and on land vehicles such as cars, motorcycles, trucks and buses. ABS prevents the wheels from locking up during braking, so the tyres keep gripping the road surface and the driver keeps control of the vehicle.

ABS is recognised as an important contribution to road safety because it keeps a vehicle steerable and stable during heavy braking. Wheels tend to slip and lock during severe braking or when braking on a slippery (wet, icy) surface. A locked wheel usually gives a long stopping distance, and the vehicle can lose steering stability: a locked front wheel cannot produce the side force needed to steer, and locked rear wheels let the car spin.

Objective of ABS (lecture statement)
ABS manipulates the wheel slip so that maximum friction is obtained and steering (lateral) stability is kept. In other words, the vehicle should stop in the shortest possible distance while keeping directional control. The ideal goal for the control design is to regulate the wheel velocity (and therefore the slip).

3.2 Wheel Slip

When a tyre transmits a braking force, the rubber in the contact patch deforms and slides a little. The wheel's circumferential speed ωR\omega RωR becomes smaller than the vehicle speed VVV. The longitudinal wheel slip is defined as:

Wheel slip (braking)
S=λ=V−ωRV(0≤S≤1)(3.1)S=\lambda=\frac{V-\omega R}{V}\qquad(0\le S\le1)\tag{3.1}S=λ=VV−ωR​(0≤S≤1)(3.1) ω = wheel angular velocity (rad/s), R = wheel rolling radius (m), V = vehicle forward velocity (m/s).
  • Free rolling (normal driving): V = ωR ⇒ S = 0.
  • Wheel lock-up (severe braking): ω = 0 while V > 0 ⇒ S = 1. Lock-up is undesirable because it lengthens the stopping distance and causes loss of directional control.
  • Slip is often quoted in percent: S = 0.2 means 20 % slip.

3.3 The μ-Slip Curve (Tyre–Road Friction Characteristic)

The friction coefficient μ=Fx/Fz\mu=F_x/F_zμ=Fx​/Fz​ that a tyre can develop depends strongly on slip. The widely used Burckhardt tyre model describes it as:

Burckhardt friction model
μ(λ)=c1(1−e−c2λ)−c3λ(3.2)\mu(\lambda)=c_1\left(1-e^{-c_2\lambda}\right)-c_3\lambda\tag{3.2}μ(λ)=c1​(1−e−c2​λ)−c3​λ(3.2) Setting dμ/dλ = 0 gives the optimal slip and peak friction: c1c2e−c2λ−c3=0 ⇒ λp=1c2ln⁡c1c2c3(3.3)c_1c_2e^{-c_2\lambda}-c_3=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda_p=\frac{1}{c_2}\ln\frac{c_1c_2}{c_3}\tag{3.3}c1​c2​e−c2​λ−c3​=0 ⇒ λp​=c2​1​lnc3​c1​c2​​(3.3)
Surfacec₁c₂c₃Optimal slip λp\lambda_{p}λp​Peak μp\mu_{p}μp​Locked μ (λ = 1)
Dry asphalt1.280123.990.520.1701.1700.760
Wet asphalt0.85733.8220.3470.1310.8010.510
Dry cobblestone1.37136.45650.66910.4001.0000.700
Snow0.194694.1290.06460.0600.1900.130
Ice0.05306.390→ saturates≈ 0.050.050

Reading the curve:

  1. Stable (linear) region, 0 < λ < λp\lambda_{p}λp​: μ rises almost linearly with slip. A small increase in brake torque gives more braking force, and the wheel stays stable.
  2. Peak at λp\lambda_{p}λp​ ≈ 0.1–0.3 on most surfaces: maximum braking force.
  3. Unstable region, λ > λp\lambda_{p}λp​: μ falls as slip increases. More slip gives less friction, so the wheel decelerates even faster and locks within a few tens of milliseconds unless the pressure is released.
  4. Lateral (side) friction μy\mu_{y}μy​ is highest at zero slip and falls towards zero as λ → 1. A locked wheel therefore cannot produce steering or stabilising side force.
Key conclusion
ABS keeps the slip in a target window around λp\lambda_{p}λp​ (typically 0.1–0.3). In this window the longitudinal braking force is near its maximum and a useful amount of lateral force remains for steering and stability.

3.4 Components of ABS

ComponentFunction
Wheel-speed sensors (one per wheel)An inductive or active Hall/magnetoresistive sensor facing a toothed pulser (tone) ring or magnetic encoder on the hub. The signal frequency is proportional to wheel speed. They detect when a wheel is about to lock.
Vehicle-velocity informationVehicle speed is usually estimated in the ECU from all four wheel speeds (the fastest wheel while braking), sometimes aided by a longitudinal accelerometer. It is needed to calculate slip.
ABS control module (ECU)Works out wheel acceleration and deceleration and slip, compares them with thresholds, and commands the valves. It monitors the system and lights the warning lamp if there is a fault.
Hydraulic modulator unitSolenoid valves (inlet and outlet for each channel), a return pump driven by an electric motor, and a low-pressure accumulator. It builds up, holds and releases the brake pressure at each wheel independently of pedal force.
Brake booster and master cylinderProduce the driver's brake pressure, which is the pressure source for the modulator.
Wheel brakes (calipers/cylinders, discs)The brake actuators that turn pressure into brake torque TbT_{b}Tb​.
Warning lampTells the driver that ABS is disabled. Normal braking without ABS remains available.

Channel configurations: 4-channel / 4-sensor (each wheel controlled separately, the best arrangement); 3-channel / 3- or 4-sensor (front wheels separately, rear axle together on the “select-low” principle); 1-channel (rear axle only, found on older light trucks).

3.5 The Hydraulic Modulator and the ABS Control Cycle

Each wheel circuit has an inlet valve (IV, normally open) between the master cylinder and the wheel brake, and an outlet valve (OV, normally closed) between the wheel brake and a low-pressure accumulator. A return pump sends the released fluid back to the master cylinder circuit. The ECU switches the valves in three basic states:

PhaseInlet valveOutlet valvePumpEffect on wheel pressure
1. Pressure build-up (normal braking)OpenClosedOffRises with pedal pressure
2. Pressure holdClosedClosed—Constant (isolated from pedal)
3. Pressure reductionClosedOpenOnFalls; fluid goes to accumulator and is pumped back
4. Pressure re-build (stepped)Pulsed openClosedOnRises gradually in small steps

This build–hold–release cycle repeats many times per second. It keeps the slip oscillating in a narrow band around the μ-slip peak. The driver feels it as a pulsing brake pedal, and the pump makes a buzzing noise.

3.6 ABS Control Loop (Bosch representation)

Control-loop elementIn ABS
Controlled system (plant)Vehicle, wheel and tyre–road contact
Controlled variableWheel speed ω and hence wheel slip λ (also wheel deceleration)
Reference variableRequired (target) slip near the μ-slip peak
ControllerABS ECU: calculates the actual slip, regulates the required slip, monitors
Actuator / manipulated variableHydraulic modulator solenoid valves / wheel brake pressure
DisturbanceRoad condition (μ changes), load changes, uneven road
Sensor (feedback)Wheel-speed sensor

3.7 Mathematical Model of ABS (Quarter-Car Model)

The lecture builds the model from two free-body diagrams: the vehicle model (car body with velocity V, weight W, normal force N and friction force FfF_{f}Ff​) and the wheel model (wheel of radius rwr_{w}rw​, angular speed ωw\omega_{w}ωw​, brake torque TbT_{b}Tb​ and friction force FfF_{f}Ff​ at the contact patch). The full derivation follows.

Assumptions
(1) Straight-line braking, no steering or lateral dynamics. (2) Quarter-car: one wheel carries ¼ of the vehicle mass (or a single-wheel “unicycle” model). (3) No aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance or load transfer (or these are lumped in). (4) Constant rolling radius R = rwr_{w}rw​. (5) Friction force given by FfF_{f}Ff​ = μ(λ)N with μ(λ) from the tyre model (3.2).

3.7.1 Step 1: Vehicle (translational) equation

Newton's second law in the direction of motion, where the only horizontal force on the vehicle is the tyre friction FfF_{f}Ff​ acting backwards:

mdVdt=−Ff(3.4)m\frac{dV}{dt}=-F_f\tag{3.4}mdtdV​=−Ff​(3.4)

Vertical equilibrium (no bounce):

N−W=0 ⇒ N=W=mg(3.5)N-W=0\ \Rightarrow\ N=W=mg\tag{3.5}N−W=0 ⇒ N=W=mg(3.5)

Tyre friction force from the tyre model:

Ff=μ(λ)N=μ(λ)mg(3.6)F_f=\mu(\lambda)N=\mu(\lambda)mg\tag{3.6}Ff​=μ(λ)N=μ(λ)mg(3.6)

Substituting (3.6) into (3.4):

Newton's second law for rotation about the axle. The brake torque TbT_{b}Tb​ opposes rotation. The friction force FfF_{f}Ff​ at the contact patch, at radius R, produces a torque FfF_{f}Ff​R that tends to keep the wheel spinning (the road “drives” the wheel):

Jdωdt=FfR−Tb(3.8)J\frac{d\omega}{dt}=F_fR-T_b\tag{3.8}Jdtdω​=Ff​R−Tb​(3.8)

ω˙=μ(λ)NR−TbJ(3.9)\dot\omega=\frac{\mu(\lambda)NR-T_b}{J}\tag{3.9}ω˙=Jμ(λ)NR−Tb​​(3.9) If Tb>μNRT_b>\mu NRTb​>μNR the wheel decelerates faster than the vehicle, so slip grows. If Tb<μNRT_b<\mu NRTb​<μNR the wheel spins back up.

Start from the definition (3.1) written as λ=1−ωR/V\lambda=1-\omega R/Vλ=1−ωR/V. Differentiate with respect to time using the quotient rule (RRR constant):

3.7.6 Step 6: Control law

  • Rule-based (bang-bang) threshold control, the classic industrial method: if λ > λmax\lambda_{\text{max}}λmax​ or wheel deceleration < −a → release. If λ < λmin\lambda_{\text{min}}λmin​ or wheel acceleration > +a → re-apply. Otherwise hold.
  • PID slip control: e=λref−λe=\lambda_{\text{ref}}-\lambdae=λref​−λ, Tcmd=Kpe+Ki∫e dt+Kde˙T_{\text{cmd}}=K_pe+K_i\int e\,dt+K_d\dot eTcmd​=Kp​e+Ki​∫edt+Kd​e˙, with λref\lambda_{\text{ref}}λref​ ≈ λp\lambda_{p}λp​ (e.g. 0.2). Pressure rises when slip is too low and falls when slip is too high.
  • Advanced: sliding-mode control (robust to unknown μ), fuzzy logic, model predictive control. μ-estimators identify the road surface and adjust λref\lambda_{\text{ref}}λref​.

3.7.7 Step 7: Simulation block diagram

3.8 Can ABS Eliminate Skidding Completely? Limitations

No. ABS reduces skidding but cannot eliminate it completely
  1. Physical friction limit: ABS can only use the friction that exists (μp\mu_{p}μp​N). If the driver asks for more (too fast for a bend, or ice), the car still slides. ABS does not create grip.
  2. Only works in braking: ABS does nothing against skids caused by acceleration (that is TCS) or by excessive cornering or yaw (that is ESP).
  3. Controlled slip exists: ABS deliberately allows 10–30 % slip and cycles around it. Brief micro-slip always remains.
  4. Low speed: ABS is disabled below ≈ 5–7 km/h, so the wheels may lock just before stopping.
  5. Loose surfaces (gravel, deep snow): a locked wheel builds a wedge of material that helps stopping, which ABS prevents. The stopping distance may be longer with ABS.
  6. Aquaplaning and sudden μ changes: with a water film, there is no tyre–road contact to control. Estimating μ and the vehicle speed takes time.
  7. Split-μ roads cause a yaw moment. The driver must counter-steer, or yaw-moment build-up delay (GMA) is used.
  8. System faults (sensor failure, modulator fault): ABS switches off and the warning lamp lights. Worn tyres or brakes also reduce effectiveness.

3.10 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q6(a)What is an Anti-lock Braking System (ABS)? How does an ABS work? Can ABS completely eliminate skidding during braking?15Topic: ABS working · skidding

Definition: ABS is an anti-skid safety braking system that prevents the wheels from locking during braking. The tyres keep gripping the road, so the vehicle remains steerable and stable, and the stopping distance on most surfaces is minimised. Its objective is to regulate wheel slip near the value that gives maximum friction while keeping lateral stability.

Components (draw Fig. 3.2 or a vehicle layout): wheel-speed sensors with pulser rings at each wheel, the ABS ECU (control module), the hydraulic modulator (inlet/outlet solenoid valves, return pump, accumulator), the brake booster and master cylinder, the wheel brakes and the warning lamp.

Working:

  1. Normal braking: the inlet valves are open and the outlet valves closed, so pedal pressure reaches the brakes directly and ABS stays passive.
  2. Monitoring: the ECU reads all wheel speeds continuously, estimates vehicle speed, and calculates each wheel's slip λ = (V − ωR)/V and its deceleration.
  3. Lock-up tendency detected: when a wheel decelerates too quickly or its slip exceeds the threshold (it is passing the μ-slip peak), the ECU first closes the inlet valve to hold the pressure.
  4. Pressure release: if the wheel keeps slowing, the outlet valve opens and the pump returns fluid, so pressure falls. The wheel spins back up and slip drops.
  5. Re-application: once the wheel has re-accelerated, pressure is built up again in steps (inlet valve pulsed).
  6. The cycle repeats 4–10 times per second per wheel. Slip stays around 10–30 %, where braking force is near maximum and lateral force remains. The driver feels pedal pulsation.

Can ABS completely eliminate skidding? No. ABS only makes the best use of the grip available. (i) It cannot exceed the physical friction limit μp\mu_{p}μp​N, so on ice or at excessive speed in a bend the car can still slide. (ii) It acts only during braking, not against acceleration skids or yaw instabilities (those need TCS and ESP). (iii) It deliberately keeps a controlled slip and cycles around it. (iv) It is inactive below about 5–7 km/h. (v) On gravel or deep snow the stopping distance may even be longer. (vi) Aquaplaning, split-μ roads and system faults limit it further. ABS reduces skidding and keeps the car steerable; it does not eliminate skidding.

Source lectureKMS · L4–L5 – ABS (AVT L4-L5.pptx, slides 4–11) — Skidding limitations not discussed; see §3.8

5. Simulation procedure: choose parameters (e.g. m = 450 kg per quarter, J = 1.2 kg·m², R = 0.3 m, V₀ = 25 m/s, λref\lambda_{\text{ref}}λref​ = 0.2) → integrate (i), (ii), (vi) with a fixed-step solver (e.g. 1 ms) → compute λ and μ at every step → stop at V ≈ 0.5 m/s → plot V(t), ωR(t), λ(t), stopping distance. Repeat with no ABS (TbT_{b}Tb​ = constant maximum) to compare.

6. How the system works: when the driver brakes hard, TbT_{b}Tb​ rises and the wheel slows faster than the car, so λ rises. As long as λ < λref\lambda_{\text{ref}}λref​ the controller allows pressure to build. When λ exceeds λref\lambda_{\text{ref}}λref​ (past the μ peak), the controller commands the modulator to hold and then release pressure. TbT_{b}Tb​ falls below μNR\mu NRμNR, ω˙\dot\omegaω˙ becomes positive, the wheel re-accelerates and λ falls. Pressure is then re-applied. The loop keeps λ oscillating near the μ-slip peak, which gives near-maximum deceleration (≈ μp\mu_{p}μp​g) and keeps lateral grip for steering. Results typically show the ABS car stopping about 20–30 % shorter on dry asphalt than with locked wheels (see N3.2), with no lock-up.
