2024 · Q6(a)Explain the working principle of an antilock braking system (ABS). How does it prevent wheel lockup during braking?10Topic: ABS working

Principle: ABS is a closed-loop slip-control system. It keeps the braked wheel's slip λ = (V − ωR)/V in the band near the μ-slip peak (≈ 0.1–0.3), where tyre–road friction is maximum and lateral grip remains. The controlled variable is wheel speed/slip, the manipulated variable is brake pressure, and the disturbance is the road condition (Fig. 3.4).

How lock-up is prevented:

  1. Wheel-speed sensors send the ECU the speed of each wheel. The ECU computes the vehicle reference speed, the slip and the wheel deceleration.
  2. A lock-up is starting when a wheel decelerates much faster than the vehicle can (wheel deceleration beyond a threshold) or when its slip exceeds the limit.
  3. The ECU switches that wheel's modulator valves: hold (inlet closed) → release (outlet open, pump returns fluid) → re-apply (inlet pulsed) once the wheel has recovered.
  4. Releasing pressure lowers TbT_{b}Tb​ below the friction torque μNR, so the wheel accelerates again (ω˙>0\dot\omega>0ω˙>0) before it can stop rotating.
  5. Repeating this 4–10 times per second keeps each wheel rotating at slightly below vehicle speed. It never locks, so the car stays steerable and stops in a short distance.
Source lectureKMS · L4–L5 – ABS (AVT L4-L5.pptx, slides 4–11)
2024 · Q6(b)Explain the concept of wheel slip in ABS. How does the wheel slip-friction (μ-slip) curve guide the design and tuning of an effective ABS system?15Topic: wheel slip · μ-slip curve

Wheel slip. While braking, the tyre's circumferential speed ωR is lower than the vehicle speed V because the tread deforms and slides in the contact patch. Slip is λ = (V − ωR)/V. λ = 0 means free rolling (V = ωR). λ = 1 means a locked wheel (ω = 0). Braking force is only generated when there is some slip, so slip is the quantity that ABS controls. Example: V = 20 m/s and ωR = 18 m/s gives λ = 0.1.

The μ-slip curve (draw Fig. 3.1): μ rises almost linearly from 0 to a peak μp\mu_{p}μp​ at λp\lambda_{p}λp​ ≈ 0.1–0.3, then falls towards the sliding value at λ = 1. Lateral friction is highest at λ = 0 and drops sharply as slip increases.

How it guides design and tuning:

  1. Choosing the target slip: the reference slip λref\lambda_{\text{ref}}λref​ is set at or slightly below λp\lambda_{p}λp​. This maximises braking force while keeping lateral force for steering, which is why a practical window of 0.1–0.3 is used rather than exactly the peak.
  2. Stability boundary: left of the peak (dμ/dλ > 0) the wheel is self-stabilising. Right of the peak (dμ/dλ < 0) it is unstable and lock-up happens within milliseconds. The curve tells the designer that the controller must release pressure as soon as the peak is passed. This sets the release thresholds and the valve response speed needed.
  3. Surface adaptation: the peak location and height vary a great deal (dry asphalt λp\lambda_{p}λp​ ≈ 0.17, μp\mu_{p}μp​ ≈ 1.17; wet ≈ 0.13/0.80; snow ≈ 0.06/0.19; cobblestone ≈ 0.40/1.0). ABS logic therefore estimates the road condition from how the wheel responds and adapts its thresholds and pressure-rise rates (gentle steps on ice, fast build-up on dry roads).
  4. Controller gains and cycle frequency: the slope of the curve (dμ/dλ) is the plant gain in the slip dynamics (3.12). A steep slope with a sharp peak needs faster, more finely stepped pressure modulation. Gains are tuned so that the limit cycle stays within the flat top of the curve.
  5. Model-based design: tyre models fitted to the curve (Burckhardt, Pacejka) are used in simulation and hardware-in-the-loop testing to tune the ABS before road tests.
  6. Performance evaluation: comparing μp\mu_{p}μp​ with μ(λ = 1) predicts the stopping-distance gain of ABS (e.g. 1.17 vs 0.76 on dry asphalt).
Source lectureKMS · L4–L5 – ABS (AVT L4-L5.pptx, slides 5–8) — μ-slip curve not in slides; see §3.3
2024 · Q6(c)What is the role of a hydraulic modulator in ABS? Is it possible for ABS to interact with other vehicle control systems? Support your answer with a proper explanation.10Topic: hydraulic modulator · ABS interaction

Role of the hydraulic modulator: it is the actuator of the ABS. It sits between the master cylinder and the wheel brakes and changes each wheel's brake pressure according to the ECU's commands, independently of pedal force. It contains, for each channel, a normally-open inlet valve and a normally-closed outlet valve, plus a motor-driven return pump, a low-pressure accumulator and damping chambers. It provides the three ABS states: build-up (IV open, OV closed), hold (both closed) and release (IV closed, OV open, pump returns fluid to the master cylinder). It can repeat these many times per second. In ESP-equipped vehicles the modulator also has switchover and high-pressure valves, so it can build pressure even without the driver pressing the pedal.

Interaction with other systems: yes. ABS is the foundation of an integrated chassis-control system:

  • TCS uses the same wheel-speed sensors, ECU and modulator. It brakes a spinning drive wheel and asks the engine ECU over CAN to cut torque.
  • ESP adds steering-angle, yaw-rate and lateral-acceleration sensors to the ABS/TCS hardware. It brakes individual wheels to create correcting yaw moments. ABS slip control stays active underneath, so the braked wheel does not lock.
  • EBD uses the ABS valves to share brake force between front and rear axles.
  • Brake assist, hill-hold, ACC and AEB command brake pressure through the same modulator.
  • Engine and transmission ECUs, instrument cluster, airbag and navigation receive ABS wheel-speed and status messages over CAN.

So ABS works as part of a networked system that shares sensors, the actuator and data over CAN (see §6.6 for details).

Source lectureKMS · L4–L5 – ABS (AVT L4-L5.pptx, slides 10–11); L8 – Electronic Stability Program (AVT_L8.pptx, slides 6, 15) — Modulator only shown in figures; see §3.5
2023 · Q6(b)How does an antilock braking system (ABS) work? Does ABS eliminate the need for effective braking techniques? Support your answer with proper explanation.10Topic: ABS working · braking technique

How ABS works (Figures 3.2 and 3.3). A wheel-speed sensor at each wheel sends its speed to the ABS ECU, which estimates the vehicle speed and computes each wheel's slip λ=(V−ωR)/V\lambda=(V-\omega R)/Vλ=(V−ωR)/V and deceleration. In hard braking, as soon as a wheel decelerates too fast or its slip passes the threshold (beyond the μ-slip peak, §3.3), the ECU commands the hydraulic modulator: hold pressure (inlet valve closed), then release it (outlet valve open, return pump on) until the wheel speeds up again, and then re-apply it in steps. The cycle repeats 4–10 times per second for each wheel. Slip is kept near 10–30 %, where braking friction is close to its maximum and the tyre still gives side force, so the car stops quickly and stays steerable.

Does ABS eliminate the need for effective braking technique? No. ABS is an aid that prevents wheel lock; it does not replace a careful driver:

  1. It cannot create grip. The shortest stop is still limited by μpg\mu_p gμp​g (§3.8, N3.2: 37.5 m from 100 km/h on dry asphalt, far more on wet or icy roads). Safe speed and following distance remain the driver's job.
  2. The technique changes, it does not disappear. With ABS the correct emergency technique is to press the pedal hard and keep it pressed, ignoring the pulsing pedal and noise, and steer around the obstacle. Pumping the pedal, as taught for cars without ABS, interrupts the ABS control and lengthens the stop.
  3. It works only near lock-up. In normal braking ABS is inactive, so smooth, early, progressive braking is still what keeps the car stable, comfortable and economical.
  4. It has limits. On gravel or deep snow ABS can lengthen the stopping distance. It is switched off below about 5–7 km/h and does not prevent skids from too much speed in a bend (that needs ESP and a sensible speed). If it fails, it switches off and the warning lamp lights.

Conclusion: ABS makes the best use of the available friction and keeps the car steerable, but the driver must still anticipate, keep a safe distance and speed, and use the right technique: firm, continuous pressure and steering.

Source lectureKMS · L4–L5 – ABS (AVT L4-L5.pptx, slides 4–11) — Braking-technique discussion not in slides; see §3.8

4. Cruise Control ★★★

4.1 Definition and Purpose

Definition
Cruise control is an automated system that lets the driver set and maintain a steady vehicle speed without keeping the accelerator pedal pressed. Its purpose is to hold a constant speed despite external disturbances such as changes in wind or road grade. It does this by measuring the vehicle speed, comparing it with the desired (reference) speed, and automatically adjusting the throttle according to a control law.

4.2 Components

ComponentFunction
Speed sensorDetects vehicle speed (vehicle speed sensor on the transmission output, or ABS wheel-speed sensors) and sends the signal to the cruise-control module.
Control moduleMicroprocessor-based unit that receives the speed signal and the driver's set speed and adjusts throttle position to hold the desired speed. On modern cars this is a software function inside the engine ECU.
ActuatorElectric or vacuum-powered actuator that sets the throttle position according to the control module's signals (see §4.6).
SwitchesSteering-wheel or dashboard switches: ON/OFF, SET, RESUME, ACCEL (+) and COAST (−).
Release (cancel) switchesBrake-pedal switch (and clutch-pedal switch on manual cars) that disengage cruise control immediately. This is a safety requirement.

4.3 Benefits, Limitations and Considerations

Benefits (lecture)

  • Reduces driver fatigue on long trips: no constant pedal pressure.
  • Improves fuel efficiency: steady speed and smooth throttle with no unnecessary acceleration.
  • Avoids speed traps: no unintentional speeding.
  • Reduces wear and tear: smooth operation of engine, transmission and brakes.

Overall, it makes long-distance driving more comfortable, efficient and safe.

Limitations and considerations

  • Not suitable in heavy or stop-and-go traffic (conventional cruise does not see the car ahead).
  • Unsafe on wet, icy or slippery roads: throttle application may cause wheel spin, and the system may cancel.
  • Limited performance on hills: slows on climbs, overspeeds on descents (§4.6.2).
  • Risk of driver inattention and slower reaction, since the foot is away from the pedals.
  • Usually works only above a minimum speed (≈ 30–40 km/h).
  • On winding roads the constant speed may be too high for bends.
  • Needs reliable cancel functions (brake/clutch switches) and fault monitoring.

4.4 Mathematical Model

4.4.1 Physical set-up and assumptions

Assumptions
(1) Wheel and tyre inertia are negligible. (2) Friction opposing motion (rolling resistance + aerodynamic drag) is proportional to speed: FresistF_{\text{resist}}Fresist​ = bv (linearised). (3) The engine and drivetrain deliver a force u to the car directly. The internal dynamics of the engine and throttle are ignored. (4) Level road (grade is added in §4.6.2). The system then reduces to a first-order mass-damper system.

4.4.2 System (differential) equation

Sum the forces in the x-direction (forward positive) and apply Newton's second law, ΣF = ma:

u−bv=mv˙ ⇒ mv˙+bv=u(4.1)u-bv=m\dot v\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{m\dot v+bv=u}\tag{4.1}u−bv=mv˙ ⇒ mv˙+bv=u​(4.1)

Since the speed is to be controlled, the output equation is

y=v(4.2)y=v\tag{4.2}y=v(4.2)

4.4.3 State-space model

A first-order system has only one energy-storage mode, here the kinetic energy of the car, so one state variable is enough: the velocity x=vx=vx=v. From (4.1): v˙=−bmv+1mu\dot v=-\frac bmv+\frac1muv˙=−mb​v+m1​u. In the standard form x˙=Ax+Bu\dot x=Ax+Bux˙=Ax+Bu, y=Cx+Duy=Cx+Duy=Cx+Du:

State-space representation
x˙=[v˙]=[−bm][v]+[1m][u],y=[1][v]+[0][u](4.3)\dot x=[\dot v]=\left[-\frac bm\right][v]+\left[\frac1m\right][u],\qquad y=[1][v]+[0][u]\tag{4.3}x˙=[v˙]=[−mb​][v]+[m1​][u],y=[1][v]+[0][u](4.3) A=−b/mA=-b/mA=−b/m,   B=1/mB=1/mB=1/m,   C=1C=1C=1,   D=0D=0D=0.
Note on the lecture slide
The lecture slide writes the input matrix as [k/m]. With u defined as the force in newtons, the correct entry is 1/m, which matches the transfer function 1/(ms + b) on the next slide. If the throttle-to-force gain k is included (u = throttle signal, force = k·u), the entry becomes k/m and the transfer function becomes k/(ms + b). Say which convention you use in the exam.

4.4.4 Transfer function model

Take the Laplace transform of (4.1) with zero initial conditions (v(0)=0v(0)=0v(0)=0), using L{v˙}=sV(s)−v(0)\mathcal L\{\dot v\}=sV(s)-v(0)L{v˙}=sV(s)−v(0):

m[sV(s)−0]+bV(s)=U(s)m[sV(s)-0]+bV(s)=U(s)m[sV(s)−0]+bV(s)=U(s) msV(s)+bV(s)=U(s)msV(s)+bV(s)=U(s)msV(s)+bV(s)=U(s) (ms+b)V(s)=U(s)(ms+b)V(s)=U(s)(ms+b)V(s)=U(s)
Open-loop transfer function
T(s)=V(s)U(s)=1ms+b=1/bτs+1,τ=mb(4.4)T(s)=\frac{V(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{ms+b}=\frac{1/b}{\tau s+1},\qquad \tau=\frac mb\tag{4.4}T(s)=U(s)V(s)​=ms+b1​=τs+11/b​,τ=bm​(4.4) The pole is at s=−b/ms=-b/ms=−b/m, the DC gain is 1/b1/b1/b, and the time constant is τ=m/b\tau=m/bτ=m/b.

4.4.5 Open-loop step response (time domain)

For a constant force u=U0u=U_0u=U0​ (step): V(s)=U0s(ms+b)V(s)=\dfrac{U_0}{s(ms+b)}V(s)=s(ms+b)U0​​. Partial fractions:

V(s)=U0b(1s−1s+b/m) ⇒ v(t)=U0b(1−e−t/τ)(4.5)V(s)=\frac{U_0}{b}\left(\frac1s-\frac{1}{s+b/m}\right)\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{v(t)=\frac{U_0}{b}\left(1-e^{-t/\tau}\right)}\tag{4.5}V(s)=bU0​​(s1​−s+b/m1​) ⇒ v(t)=bU0​​(1−e−t/τ)​(4.5)

The final speed is U0/bU_0/bU0​/b. The car reaches 63.2 % of it at t = τ and 98 % at t = 4τ.

4.5 Cruise Control as a Feedback Control System

Feedback elementIn cruise control
Reference inputDriver's set speed vrefv_{\text{ref}}vref​
Sensor (feedback path)Vehicle speed sensor
Error detectore = vrefv_{\text{ref}}vref​ − v, computed in the ECU
ControllerPI or PID control law in the ECU
ActuatorThrottle actuator (vacuum, electric or drive-by-wire)
PlantEngine, drivetrain and vehicle mass (1/(ms + b))
DisturbanceRoad grade, head wind, extra load
Controlled outputActual vehicle speed v

4.5.1 Proportional control

Control law u=Kp(r−v)u=K_p(r-v)u=Kp​(r−v). Closed-loop transfer function:

V(s)R(s)=Kp/(ms+b)1+Kp/(ms+b)=Kpms+b+Kp(4.6)\frac{V(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{K_p/(ms+b)}{1+K_p/(ms+b)}=\frac{K_p}{ms+b+K_p}\tag{4.6}R(s)V(s)​=1+Kp​/(ms+b)Kp​/(ms+b)​=ms+b+Kp​Kp​​(4.6)

Final value theorem for a step rrr: vss=Kprb+Kpv_{ss}=\dfrac{K_pr}{b+K_p}vss​=b+Kp​Kp​r​. So there is a steady-state error ess=brb+Kpe_{ss}=\dfrac{br}{b+K_p}ess​=b+Kp​br​. The response is faster than open loop: τcl=mb+Kp\tau_{cl}=\dfrac{m}{b+K_p}τcl​=b+Kp​m​.

4.5.2 Proportional-Integral (PI) control

Control law u=Kpe+Ki∫e dtu=K_pe+K_i\int e\,dtu=Kp​e+Ki​∫edt, C(s)=Kp+Kis=Kps+KisC(s)=K_p+\dfrac{K_i}{s}=\dfrac{K_ps+K_i}{s}C(s)=Kp​+sKi​​=sKp​s+Ki​​:

V(s)R(s)=Kps+Kims2+(b+Kp)s+Ki(4.7)\frac{V(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{K_ps+K_i}{ms^2+(b+K_p)s+K_i}\tag{4.7}R(s)V(s)​=ms2+(b+Kp​)s+Ki​Kp​s+Ki​​(4.7)

At s → 0 the gain is KiK_{i}Ki​/KiK_{i}Ki​ = 1, so there is zero steady-state error, even with a constant disturbance such as a hill. This is why practical cruise controllers use PI or PID.

4.6 Throttle Actuation Mechanisms and Hilly Terrain

4.6.1 Throttle actuation mechanisms

TypeConstruction and workingRemarks
1. Vacuum-servo actuator (older cars)A diaphragm chamber is linked to the throttle by a cable or chain. Two solenoid valves controlled by the cruise module work it: a vacuum valve admits intake-manifold vacuum to pull the diaphragm and open the throttle, and a vent valve admits atmospheric air to let it close. By pulsing these valves (PWM) the module holds any throttle position. A safety dump valve on the brake pedal vents the chamber instantly.Simple and cheap. Response depends on engine vacuum (weak at high load and on hills).
2. Electric motor actuatorA DC or stepper motor with a reduction gear and an electromagnetic clutch winds a cable or linkage connected to the throttle. A position sensor (potentiometer) gives feedback. When cruise is cancelled the clutch releases and the return spring closes the throttle.More precise than vacuum, independent of vacuum, but still an add-on mechanism.
3. Electronic throttle control (drive-by-wire) (modern)There is no mechanical link. The accelerator pedal has position sensors, and the throttle body has a DC motor with dual throttle-position sensors. Cruise control is a software function: it sends a torque/throttle request to the engine ECU, which positions the throttle motor. It also coordinates with TCS/ESP torque reduction and transmission shifting.Most accurate and smooth. Needs no extra hardware. Integrates easily with ACC.
4. Diesel / EV variantsDiesel engines have no throttle to control load, so cruise control commands the injected fuel quantity. EVs command motor torque through the inverter and can also brake regeneratively.Same control loop, different actuator.

4.6.2 Cruise control on hilly terrain: model and challenges

On a road with gradient angle θ, the weight component mgsin⁡θmg\sin\thetamgsinθ acts along the road:

Model with grade disturbance
mv˙+bv=u−mgsin⁡θ(4.8)m\dot v+bv=u-mg\sin\theta\tag{4.8}mv˙+bv=u−mgsinθ(4.8) With P control, the steady speed drop caused by the hill is Δv=mgsin⁡θb+Kp\Delta v=\dfrac{mg\sin\theta}{b+K_p}Δv=b+Kp​mgsinθ​. PI control removes it.

Challenges:

  1. Large, varying disturbance: a 5 % grade needs ≈ 490 N of extra force for a 1000 kg car, which is as much as the entire drag force at cruising speed. The grade also changes continuously.
  2. Actuator saturation uphill: the engine may be unable to deliver the needed power at full throttle, so speed drops regardless. Integrator wind-up then builds a large integral term, which causes overshoot at the crest. Anti-windup is needed.
  3. Overspeed downhill: a throttle-only system cannot produce negative force beyond engine braking. The car accelerates beyond the set speed unless the system can downshift or use the brakes (ACC-type systems).
  4. Gear-shift interaction: automatic transmissions may “hunt” between gears on hills. Cruise control and the transmission ECU must coordinate shift points.
  5. Response trade-off: high gains track speed tightly but give jerky throttle and poor comfort and economy. Low gains let speed vary.
  6. Fuel economy: holding exact speed on hills wastes fuel through hard acceleration uphill. Predictive (GPS/map-based) cruise control lets speed dip slightly uphill and recover downhill, saving fuel.
  7. Mass uncertainty: passengers, luggage and trailers change m, and so change the plant dynamics. Robust or adaptive tuning is required.
  8. Vacuum-type actuators lose authority at high engine load, which is exactly the uphill condition.

4.7 Adaptive Cruise Control and ESP Interaction

Adaptive cruise control (ACC) adds a forward-looking radar (or camera/LiDAR) that measures the distance and relative speed of the vehicle ahead. If there is no vehicle ahead it holds the set speed (speed control). If there is a slower vehicle it switches to distance (time-gap) control, using both the throttle and the brakes. Stop-and-go ACC can bring the car to a stop and restart it.

ESP interaction with cruise control (lecture): during cruise control, ESP keeps monitoring wheel speeds, steering angle, yaw rate and lateral acceleration. If wheel-speed differences appear because of cornering, road conditions or wheel slip, ESP can brake individual wheels to create the right yaw moment and keep the intended path without necessarily changing the target cruising speed. ESP can therefore interrupt normal cruise operation with extra braking when needed, while working with the cruise system to maintain the desired speed and stable motion.

4.9 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q7(a)What is Cruise Control? What are the limitations and considerations when using Cruise Control? Can Cruise Control contribute to fuel efficiency?10Topic: cruise control

Cruise control is an automated system that lets the driver set and hold a steady speed without pressing the accelerator. It measures the vehicle speed, compares it with the set speed and automatically adjusts the throttle through a control law, to hold the speed despite disturbances such as grade and wind. Components: speed sensor, control module, throttle actuator and driver switches (ON/OFF, SET, RESUME, ±), plus brake/clutch cancel switches.

Limitations and considerations: (1) Not suitable in dense or stop-and-go traffic, since it cannot see other vehicles (unless it is adaptive). (2) Dangerous on wet, icy or snowy roads: throttle application can cause wheel spin or aquaplaning, so it should be switched off. (3) On hills it slows uphill (actuator saturation) and overspeeds downhill (no braking). (4) On winding roads the set speed may be too high for bends. (5) Driver complacency and slower reaction, since the foot is off the pedals. (6) Works only above a minimum speed (≈ 30–40 km/h). (7) Needs reliable cancel switches and fault detection, and the driver stays responsible at all times.

Fuel efficiency: yes, under the right conditions. Fuel is wasted mainly by unnecessary acceleration and braking. On flat highways, cruise control holds a steady speed with smooth, small throttle changes, avoids speed fluctuations and keeps the engine near an efficient operating point. Studies typically show savings of a few percent up to about 7 %. On hilly roads a conventional cruise control can use more fuel, because it accelerates hard to hold speed uphill. Predictive or eco cruise control, which lets speed vary slightly, recovers the saving.

Source lectureKMS · L6 – Cruise Control (AVT_L6(2)(1).pdf, pp. 4–6) — Limitations/considerations not in slides
2022 · Q7(b)Explain – “Automatic Cruise Control is an excellent example of a feedback control system in modern vehicles.”05Topic: cruise control as feedback

A feedback (closed-loop) system measures its output, compares it with the desired value and uses the error to correct the input. Cruise control contains every element of such a loop (draw Fig. 4.2): the reference input is the driver's set speed. The sensor measures the actual speed. The error detector in the ECU computes e = vrefv_{\text{ref}}vref​ − v. The controller (PI) computes the throttle command. The actuator positions the throttle. The plant is the engine and vehicle (mv˙+bv=um\dot v+bv=umv˙+bv=u). Disturbances are grade and wind. When a hill slows the car, the error grows and the controller opens the throttle. When the car overspeeds, the throttle closes. The speed is held automatically without the driver. Because it clearly shows negative feedback, disturbance rejection and (with PI) zero steady-state error, it is a standard textbook example of feedback control.

Source lectureKMS · L6 – Cruise Control (AVT_L6(2)(1).pdf, pp. 4–10) — Closed-loop controller (P/PI) not in slides; see §4.5
2024 · Q7(a)What is cruise control? Describe the throttle actuation mechanisms used in cruise control systems. Discuss the challenges of designing cruise control for hilly terrains.15Topic: cruise control · throttle actuation

Cruise control is a closed-loop speed-control system that holds a driver-selected speed without accelerator input. It compares the measured speed with the set speed and adjusts the throttle through a control law (usually PI). Model: mv˙+bv=um\dot v+bv=umv˙+bv=u; T(s) = 1/(ms + b). Components: speed sensor, control module, throttle actuator and switches.

Throttle actuation mechanisms:

  1. Vacuum-servo actuator: a diaphragm servo connected to the throttle by a cable. A vacuum solenoid valve lets manifold vacuum pull the diaphragm (opening the throttle), and a vent valve lets in air (closing it). The module pulses both valves to hold position. A brake-pedal dump valve releases it instantly. It is cheap, but its force depends on manifold vacuum.
  2. Electric motor actuator: a DC or stepper motor with gears and an electromagnetic clutch pulls the throttle cable. A feedback potentiometer reports position. The clutch disengages on cancel so the spring closes the throttle. More accurate and independent of vacuum.
  3. Electronic throttle control (drive-by-wire): there is no cable. Cruise control is software in the engine ECU, which drives the throttle-body DC motor using redundant throttle-position sensors. It gives the most accurate, smooth control and integrates with TCS, ESP, the transmission and ACC.
  4. In diesel engines the fuel quantity is commanded; in EVs the motor torque (including regenerative braking).

Challenges on hilly terrain (model: mv˙+bv=u−mgsin⁡θm\dot v+bv=u-mg\sin\thetamv˙+bv=u−mgsinθ):

  1. The grade force mg sinθ is a large, time-varying disturbance (≈ 490 N on a 5 % grade for 1000 kg). P control leaves a speed drop Δv = mg sinθ/(b + KpK_{p}Kp​), so integral action is needed.
  2. Uphill the engine may reach full throttle (saturation) and speed falls anyway. Integrator wind-up then causes overshoot over the crest, so anti-windup is required.
  3. Downhill, a throttle-only system cannot brake. The car overspeeds unless it downshifts or uses the brakes.
  4. Gear hunting in automatic transmissions needs coordination with the TCU.
  5. Vacuum actuators lose force exactly when load is high.
  6. Trade-off between tight speed tracking and comfort and fuel economy. Aggressive throttle uphill wastes fuel, which predictive (map/GPS-based) cruise control addresses.
  7. Vehicle mass and load vary (passengers, trailer), so the controller must be robust.
Source lectureKMS · L6 – Cruise Control (AVT_L6(2)(1).pdf, pp. 4–5) — Hilly-terrain challenges not in slides; see §4.6.2

Step 5: Practical features. Throttle saturation with anti-windup (stop integrating when the actuator is at its limit); works only above about 40 km/h; set / resume / accelerate / coast switches; cancel on the brake or clutch pedal or the off switch; ramp-limit the set-speed changes for comfort; share data with ESP over CAN (§4.7). An optional radar adds adaptive cruise control.

Step 6: How the system works. The driver reaches the desired speed and presses SET; the ECU stores it as rrr. Every few milliseconds the ECU reads the vehicle speed, forms the error e=r−ve=r-ve=r−v and computes u=Kpe+Ki∫e dtu=K_pe+K_i\int e\,dtu=Kp​e+Ki​∫edt. The throttle actuator opens or closes the throttle to produce that force. If the car slows on a hill, eee becomes positive, the proportional term opens the throttle at once and the integral term keeps adding force until the error is zero. Downhill the throttle closes (and some systems also use the brakes). Pressing the brake cancels the system, and RESUME returns to the stored speed.

5. Traction Control System (TCS) ★★★

5.1 Definition

Definition (lecture)
A traction control system (TCS), also called ASR (German Antriebsschlupfregelung, “drive slippage regulation”), prevents loss of traction (wheel spin) of the driven wheels. It is usually, though not necessarily, a secondary function of the electronic stability control (ESC). TCS is activated when the throttle input and the engine power and torque transfer do not match the road surface conditions. It detects when one or more wheels lose traction and then automatically reduces engine power or applies the brake to that wheel to restore traction.

TCS is the “mirror image” of ABS. ABS stops wheels from locking under braking (brake slip rising towards 1, wheel slower than the car). TCS stops driven wheels from spinning under acceleration (positive drive slip). It is especially useful in slippery or wet conditions such as snow, ice or rain. By preventing wheel spin it helps the driver keep control and reduces the risk of accidents. Less wheel slip can also mean better traction, better handling and improved fuel economy.

5.2 Drive Slip

Drive (traction) slip
λd=ωR−VωR(5.1)\lambda_d=\frac{\omega R-V}{\omega R}\tag{5.1}λd​=ωRωR−V​(5.1) λd=0\lambda_d=0λd​=0: rolling without slip. λd→1\lambda_d\to1λd​→1: wheel spinning on the spot (V ≈ 0). As in braking, traction force peaks at a drive slip of ≈ 0.1–0.3. Beyond that, traction falls and lateral grip is lost: a spinning rear axle makes the car oversteer, and a spinning front axle loses steering.

In practice the ECU compares each driven wheel's speed with the non-driven wheels, which give the vehicle reference speed (or with an accelerometer-based vehicle speed on 4WD cars). If a driven wheel runs clearly faster, it is spinning.

5.3 Why Modern Vehicles Use TCS (lecture)

  • Comfort: smooth take-off without wheel spin, jerks or driver correction.
  • Safety: keeps the car stable and steerable when accelerating on slippery or split-μ roads and in bends.
  • Fuel economy: engine energy is not wasted spinning wheels.
  • Regulatory requirements: ESC, which includes TCS, is mandatory in many markets.
  • Improved handling: maximum usable traction, especially in powerful rear-wheel-drive cars.
  • Less tyre wear and less drivetrain shock.

5.4 Components and Schematic

ComponentFunction
Wheel-speed sensorsMounted at each wheel. They measure rotational speed and tell the TCS module when a wheel is slipping. (Shared with ABS.)
AccelerometerMeasures vehicle acceleration, from which vehicle speed is obtained and compared with wheel speed. This is important for 4WD, where no wheel is free-rolling.
TCS control moduleThe brain of the TCS. It takes the wheel-speed and other sensor data and calculates how much engine power reduction and/or brake pressure to apply at each wheel.
Engine control unit (ECU)Controls the engine and carries out the TCS module's torque-reduction commands received over CAN.
Brake system (ABS modulator)Applies pressure to a slipping wheel to bring it back into traction. The TCS module works with the ABS module to control each wheel's brake pressure.
Accelerator-pedal sensorDetects pedal position and sends it to the TCS module. If the driver presses too hard for the road conditions, TCS may intervene.
TCS indicator / OFF switchA lamp flashes during intervention. The switch lets the driver disable TCS (e.g. to rock the car free in deep snow).

5.5 Role of Wheel-Speed Sensors in TCS

  • Basic function: each sensor measures the rotational speed of its wheel continuously. They are the primary input of TCS: comparing the speeds of driven and non-driven wheels (or with the accelerometer-derived speed) is how wheel spin is detected, and the size of the difference decides how strongly TCS intervenes.
  • Passive (inductive) sensor: a permanent magnet with a coil faces a steel toothed ring. Each passing tooth changes the magnetic flux and induces an AC voltage whose frequency is proportional to wheel speed. It needs no power supply, but the signal is weak at low speed (it cannot measure below ≈ 2–5 km/h).
  • Active (Hall-effect / magnetoresistive) sensor: powered, it reads a multipole magnetic encoder ring and outputs a square-wave current signal. It measures down to zero speed, detects direction, and is smaller and less sensitive to air gap. This is the modern standard and is needed for hill-start assist and low-speed TCS.
  • Information derived: wheel speed, wheel acceleration (dω/dt, to detect spin quickly), vehicle reference speed, drive slip, detection of split-μ (only one side spinning) and cornering (inner and outer wheels differ).
  • Shared use: the same sensors serve ABS, TCS, ESP, EBD, the speedometer and odometer, hill-hold, the tyre-deflation warning and navigation.

5.6 TCS Intervention Strategies

5.6.1 Engine torque reduction strategies

StrategyHow it worksResponse / remarks
1. Throttle-valve closing (electronic throttle)The engine ECU closes the drive-by-wire throttle below the driver's pedal command, reducing air and so torque.Smooth, but slow (≈ 100–300 ms, because the manifold must empty).
2. Ignition-timing retardThe spark is fired later than optimal, so combustion does less work and torque drops.Very fast (next combustion event). Used for quick short-term cuts. Raises exhaust temperature, so it is time-limited to protect the catalyst.
3. Fuel-injection cut-off (cylinder suppression)Injection is cut to one or more cylinders (selective cylinder cut-out).Fast and strong. Coarse steps; can stress the catalyst.
4. Diesel: reduced fuel quantityThe ECU lowers the injected quantity directly.Fast and smooth.
5. Turbo boost reductionThe wastegate or VGT reduces boost pressure.Slow. Supports the other methods.
6. EV / hybrid: motor torque reductionThe inverter reduces motor torque within milliseconds.Fastest and most precise.
7. Transmission interventionUpshift or hold a higher gear to reduce wheel torque.Supporting measure.

A typical strategy combines a fast action (ignition retard or injection cut) to stop the spin at once with a slow action (throttle closing) to hold the reduced torque smoothly.

5.6.2 Brake intervention (electronic differential lock)

On a split-μ road (one wheel on ice, the other on asphalt), an open differential sends equal torque to both wheels, limited by the wheel on ice. The ice wheel spins and the car hardly moves. TCS brakes the spinning wheel. The brake torque acts as a reaction for the differential, so the same extra torque is transferred to the wheel with grip. This works like a limited-slip or locking differential (“brake-based EDL”). It is used mainly at low speed. At higher speed, engine intervention is preferred to avoid overheating the brakes.

5.7 ABS vs TCS

PointABSTCS
Acts duringBrakingAcceleration / driving
PreventsWheel lock-upWheel spin
Slip definitionλ = (V − ωR)/Vλd\lambda_{d}λd​ = (ωR − V)/(ωR)
Wheels controlledAll wheelsDriven wheels
ActuatorsBrake modulator (reduces pressure)Engine torque reduction + brake modulator (builds pressure)
HardwareWheel sensors, ECU, modulatorSame, plus engine interface; modulator must build pressure without the pedal

5.8 Solved Past Questions

2024 · Q7(b)Describe the role of wheel speed sensors in the Traction Control System (TCS). Discuss the engine torque reduction strategies used in TCS.10Topic: TCS sensors · torque reduction

Role of wheel-speed sensors:

  1. They are the main input of TCS. A sensor at each wheel (inductive, or active Hall/magnetoresistive facing a tone or encoder ring) produces a signal whose frequency is proportional to wheel speed.
  2. Spin detection: the TCS ECU compares each driven wheel's speed with the non-driven wheels (the vehicle reference speed) or with the accelerometer-based speed. A driven wheel turning faster is spinning, and its drive slip is λd\lambda_{d}λd​ = (ωR − V)/ωR.
  3. Intervention decision and dosing: the size of the slip and the wheel acceleration dω/dt tell the ECU when to act, and whether to reduce engine torque (both wheels spinning) or brake one wheel (only one wheel spinning on split-μ).
  4. Closed-loop feedback: during intervention the sensors show whether slip has returned to the target (≈ 10–20 %) so torque can be restored smoothly.
  5. Active sensors measure down to zero speed, so TCS works even at take-off. The same sensors also serve ABS, ESP and the speedometer.

Engine torque reduction strategies: (i) throttle closing via electronic throttle: smooth but slow; (ii) ignition retard: very fast, next combustion, time-limited because of catalyst temperature; (iii) fuel-injection cut-off to selected cylinders: fast, strong reduction; (iv) in diesels, reduced injection quantity; (v) turbo boost reduction; (vi) in EVs and hybrids, motor torque reduction via the inverter; (vii) transmission upshift. Fast methods (ignition, fuel) stop the spin at once, and throttle reduction then holds the lower torque. When only one wheel spins, TCS also brakes that wheel through the ABS modulator, which sends torque to the wheel with grip. The TCS ECU sends its torque-reduction request to the engine ECU over CAN.

Source lectureKMS · L7 – Traction Control System (AVT TCS.pptx, slides 5–10) — Specific torque-reduction methods (spark retard, fuel cut) not detailed
2023 · Q7(a)What is traction control system (TCS)? How does a TCS work? Is it only beneficial to drive on slippery surfaces?10Topic: TCS working and benefits

TCS (ASR, “drive slippage regulation”) is an active safety system that prevents the driven wheels from spinning when the engine torque is more than the road can transmit, for example when the driver accelerates on a slippery surface. It is usually a function of the ESC/ABS unit (§5.1).

How it works (draw Figure 5.2):

  1. The four wheel-speed sensors (shared with ABS) report each wheel's speed. The undriven wheels and the accelerometer give the vehicle speed VVV.
  2. The TCS module computes the drive slip λd=(ωR−V)/(ωR)\lambda_d=(\omega R-V)/(\omega R)λd​=(ωR−V)/(ωR) (5.1). If a driven wheel turns clearly faster than the vehicle, it is spinning.
  3. Engine torque reduction: over CAN, the TCS asks the engine ECU to reduce torque by closing the electronic throttle, retarding the ignition or cutting injection to some cylinders (§5.6.1).
  4. Brake intervention: through the ABS modulator it builds pressure at the spinning wheel. On split-μ roads this transfers torque through the differential to the wheel with grip (electronic differential lock, §5.6.2).
  5. When the slip returns to the target range (about 10–20 %), the intervention is removed and the driver gets full torque again. A warning lamp flashes while TCS is active.

Is it only beneficial on slippery surfaces? No. It is most noticeable on snow, ice and rain (lecture), but it helps in many other situations:

  • Hard acceleration on dry roads with a powerful engine, especially rear-wheel drive: it prevents wheel spin, so the car accelerates harder and does not snap sideways.
  • Accelerating in a bend: a spinning wheel loses side grip. TCS keeps lateral grip and prevents power oversteer (rear-wheel drive) or understeer (front-wheel drive).
  • Split-μ and loose surfaces: one wheel on gravel, sand, a painted line or a wet patch. Brake intervention gives traction at the other wheel.
  • Hill starts and towing: controlled take-off without wheel spin.
  • Comfort, tyre wear, fuel economy and drivetrain protection: no wasted energy or tyre rubber, and no shock loads when a spinning wheel suddenly grips (lecture, §5.3).
  • Regulatory requirement: it is part of ESC, which is mandatory for new cars in many markets.
Source lectureKMS · L7 – Traction Control System (AVT TCS.pptx, slides 4–10)

6. Electronic Stability Program (ESP / ESC) ★★★

6.1 Definition and Purpose

Definition (lecture)
The Electronic Stability Program (ESP), also called Electronic Stability Control (ESC), is a safety feature of modern cars that improves stability and control during driving manoeuvres. In critical situations this computerised system helps the driver keep control of the vehicle by automatically braking individual wheels and adjusting engine power.

ESP continuously monitors steering angle, vehicle speed, wheel rotation, yaw rate and lateral acceleration. If it detects a loss of control, meaning the vehicle is leaving the path the driver intends, it intervenes to correct the situation. When it detects understeer (the vehicle does not turn enough) or oversteer (the rear of the vehicle starts to slide out), it selectively brakes specific wheels and reduces engine power to stabilise the vehicle and bring it back under the driver's control. This helps prevent skidding, sliding and loss of control, particularly on slippery roads or in emergencies.

ESP has become a standard safety feature in many vehicles and has reduced the number of accidents caused by loss of control. It works together with ABS and TCS to improve overall vehicle stability and driver safety.

Why modern vehicles use ESP (lecture): enhanced vehicle safety · improved traction and stability · mitigation of understeer and oversteer · effective counteraction of skidding · increased driver confidence and assistance.

6.2 Understeer and Oversteer

ConditionWhat happensYaw rate compared with referenceESP action
UndersteerFront tyres lose lateral grip first. The car turns less than steered and “pushes” toward the outside of the bend.|ψ˙actual\dot\psi_{\text{actual}}ψ˙​actual​| < |ψ˙ref\dot\psi_{\text{ref}}ψ˙​ref​| (yaw deficit)Brake the inner rear wheel (and inner front if needed), reduce engine torque ⇒ yaw moment into the bend.
OversteerRear tyres lose grip first. The rear slides out and the car rotates more than steered, and may spin.|ψ˙actual\dot\psi_{\text{actual}}ψ˙​actual​| > |ψ˙ref\dot\psi_{\text{ref}}ψ˙​ref​| (yaw excess), large side-slip angle βBrake the outer front wheel ⇒ yaw moment out of the bend (counter-rotation).

6.3 How ESP Detects Understeer and Oversteer: the Reference Yaw Rate

ESP compares the driver's intention with the actual vehicle motion:

  • Driver's intention comes from the steering-angle sensor (δ), the vehicle speed (from wheel speeds) and the brake/accelerator pedal (brake-pressure sensor, engine data).
  • Actual motion comes from the yaw-rate sensor (ψ˙\dot\psiψ˙​, rotation about the vertical axis), the lateral-acceleration sensor (aya_{y}ay​) and the wheel speeds. From these the ECU estimates the side-slip angle β.

6.3.1 Derivation of the reference (desired) yaw rate: single-track (bicycle) model

Step 1: Geometry. At low speed a car with wheelbase L and road-wheel steering angle δ follows a circle of radius Rt=L/δR_t=L/\deltaRt​=L/δ (Ackermann steering, small angles).
Step 2: Understeer at speed. At higher speed the tyres need slip angles. Steady-state cornering theory gives δ=LRt+Kusay\delta=\dfrac{L}{R_t}+K_{us}a_yδ=Rt​L​+Kus​ay​, where KusK_{us}Kus​ is the understeer gradient (>0>0>0 for a normal understeering car).
Step 3: Kinematics. In steady turning, V=Rtψ˙ ⇒ 1/Rt=ψ˙/VV=R_t\dot\psi\ \Rightarrow\ 1/R_t=\dot\psi/VV=Rt​ψ˙​ ⇒ 1/Rt​=ψ˙​/V, and ay=Vψ˙a_y=V\dot\psiay​=Vψ˙​.
Step 4: Substitute. δ=Lψ˙V+KusVψ˙=ψ˙ (L+KusV2)V\delta=\dfrac{L\dot\psi}{V}+K_{us}V\dot\psi=\dfrac{\dot\psi\,(L+K_{us}V^2)}{V}δ=VLψ˙​​+Kus​Vψ˙​=Vψ˙​(L+Kus​V2)​.
Reference yaw rate
ψ˙ref=VL+KusV2 δ,limited by∣ψ˙ref∣≤μgV(6.1)\dot\psi_{\text{ref}}=\frac{V}{L+K_{us}V^2}\,\delta,\qquad\text{limited by}\quad|\dot\psi_{\text{ref}}|\le\frac{\mu g}{V}\tag{6.1}ψ˙​ref​=L+Kus​V2V​δ,limited by∣ψ˙​ref​∣≤Vμg​(6.1) The limit comes from ay=Vψ˙≤μga_y=V\dot\psi\le\mu gay​=Vψ˙​≤μg: the tyres cannot give more lateral acceleration than the road friction allows.
Step 5: Decision. Yaw-rate error Δψ˙=ψ˙actual−ψ˙ref\Delta\dot\psi=\dot\psi_{\text{actual}}-\dot\psi_{\text{ref}}Δψ˙​=ψ˙​actual​−ψ˙​ref​ (sign taken in the turning direction).
• Δψ˙<−\Delta\dot\psi<-Δψ˙​<−threshold ⇒ understeer. • Δψ˙>+\Delta\dot\psi>+Δψ˙​>+threshold ⇒ oversteer. • A large or fast-growing side-slip angle β also signals oversteer, even if the yaw error is small.
Step 6: Corrective yaw moment. A braking force FbF_{b}Fb​ on one wheel at half-track distance t/2 from the centreline produces a yaw moment Mz=Fb⋅t/2M_z=F_b\cdot t/2Mz​=Fb​⋅t/2. The ESP controller computes the required MzM_zMz​ from the yaw error and chooses the wheel and brake pressure. The ABS slip controller underneath makes sure that wheel does not lock.

6.4 ESP Control Loop and Components

Component (lecture)Role in ESP
SensorsWheel-speed sensors measure each wheel's rotation. Yaw-rate sensor and lateral-acceleration sensor (gyroscopic/MEMS) give the actual vehicle motion in real time. A brake-pressure sensor gives the driver's braking demand.
Electronic control unitThe central module. It receives the sensor data, continuously evaluates vehicle stability (driver's intention vs actual motion) and activates or modulates the other components.
Traction control systemWorks with ESP to prevent wheel spin during acceleration, using the ABS sensors and applying brake force to specific wheels.
Steering-angle sensor (SAS)Measures the angle and direction of the steering wheel, which is the driver's intended direction. This is essential for detecting mismatches between intended and actual motion.
Engine management system (EMS)Regulates engine torque and power (throttle, ignition, injection) on ESP request, to stabilise the car when loss of control is imminent.
Hydraulic modulatorAn ABS modulator extended with switchover and high-pressure valves, so ESP can actively build brake pressure at any single wheel without the driver pressing the pedal.

6.5 ESP Behaviour in Typical Manoeuvres (lecture figures)

ManoeuvreWithout ESPWith ESP
Cornering with oversteerRear breaks away and the vehicle skids or spins.ESP brakes the outer front wheel, which reduces the risk of skidding.
Cornering with understeerFront breaks away and the vehicle leaves the road at the outside of the bend.ESP brakes the inner rear wheel, which reduces understeer.
Right–left cornering sequence (lane change / obstacle avoidance)Phase 1 driver steers; 2 incipient instability; 3 driver counter-steers and loses control; 4 vehicle becomes uncontrollable.Phase 2: intervention at left front; phase 3: vehicle remains under control; phase 4: intervention at right front, complete stabilisation.
Lane change during emergency brakingWith ABS only, the car follows the lane change but yaws strongly and may swerve.ESP distributes brake force per wheel and completes the lane change with stable tracking.
Rapid steering and counter-steering with increasing anglesSwing-out grows with each input and the car spins.Vehicle tracks the slalom path.
Cornering while braking (constant steering)Car turns in (oversteer) or runs wide.Increased and decreased brake forces on individual wheels keep the line.
Cornering while acceleratingDrive slip causes the car to run wide or spin.Engine torque reduction plus wheel braking keep the line.

6.6 Integration and Interaction of ABS, TCS and ESP

  • Shared hardware: ABS, TCS and ESP are usually one integrated unit (ECU plus hydraulic modulator) using the same four wheel-speed sensors. TCS adds the ability to build pressure and to talk to the engine ECU. ESP adds the steering-angle, yaw-rate and lateral-acceleration sensors and a pressure sensor.
  • Layered (hierarchical) control: ESP is the top-level controller. It decides a desired yaw moment and gives slip targets to the ABS/TCS slip controllers, which carry them out at wheel level. ABS always stays active, so a wheel braked by ESP never locks.
  • During braking: ABS keeps each wheel near optimal slip. ESP can change the per-wheel slip targets (e.g. more brake on the outer front) to correct yaw while braking. EBD sets front/rear distribution.
  • During acceleration: TCS limits drive slip. ESP uses the same torque-reduction and brake-intervention channels to correct under- or oversteer.
  • Engine drag torque control (EDTC): when the driver lifts off or downshifts on a slippery road, engine braking can make the driven wheels slip (like braking). The system raises engine torque slightly to prevent this.
  • Communication: the integrated unit exchanges data over CAN with the engine ECU (torque requests), the transmission (shift inhibits), the instrument cluster (warning lamps), ACC/cruise control, airbag and navigation.

6.8 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q7(c)Write short notes on: (i) Traction Control Systems (TCS), (ii) Electronic Stability Program (ESP).10Topic: TCS · ESP

(i) Traction Control System (TCS / ASR): an active safety system that prevents the driven wheels from spinning when the driver accelerates on slippery surfaces, i.e. when engine torque exceeds what the road can transmit. The wheel-speed sensors (shared with ABS) and an accelerometer let the TCS ECU compare driven and non-driven wheel speeds. A driven wheel running faster than the others is spinning (drive slip λd\lambda_{d}λd​ = (ωR − V)/ωR). The ECU then (a) asks the engine ECU to reduce torque by closing the throttle, retarding ignition or cutting injection, and/or (b) uses the ABS modulator to brake the spinning wheel, which also sends torque to the wheel with grip on split-μ roads. Benefits: safety and control on snow, ice and rain, comfort, better handling, fuel economy and regulatory compliance. Components: wheel-speed sensors, accelerometer, TCS module, engine ECU, brake system and accelerator-pedal sensor.

(ii) Electronic Stability Program (ESP / ESC): a computerised active safety system that keeps the vehicle on the driver's intended path during critical manoeuvres. It monitors steering angle (the driver's intention) and yaw rate, lateral acceleration and wheel speeds (the actual motion), and compares the actual yaw rate with a reference yaw rate computed from steering angle and speed. On understeer (yaw deficit) it brakes the inner rear wheel and reduces engine torque. On oversteer (yaw excess, rear sliding) it brakes the outer front wheel. The resulting yaw moment turns the vehicle back onto the intended path. Components: wheel-speed, steering-angle, yaw-rate, lateral-acceleration and brake-pressure sensors, the ESP ECU, the hydraulic modulator, and an engine-management interface. ESP builds on ABS and TCS and has greatly reduced loss-of-control accidents. It is now standard or mandatory in many countries.

Source lectureKMS · L7 – Traction Control System (AVT TCS.pptx, slides 4–10); L8 – Electronic Stability Program (AVT_L8.pptx, slides 4–7)
2022 · Q7(d)How does ABS interact with other vehicle control systems, such as TCS and ESP?10Topic: ABS–TCS–ESP interaction

ABS, TCS and ESP form a layered, integrated brake-control system (draw the nested diagram of §6.6):

  1. Shared sensors: all three use the same four wheel-speed sensors. ABS uses them for brake slip, TCS for drive slip, and ESP for vehicle speed and wheel-slip information.
  2. Shared actuator: one hydraulic modulator. ABS uses it to reduce pressure. TCS and ESP need it to build pressure at an individual wheel without the pedal, so the modulator gets extra switchover and high-pressure valves and a stronger pump.
  3. Shared ECU and software layers: usually one control unit. ESP is the top-level yaw controller and sends slip or brake-torque targets to the lower ABS/TCS slip controllers. ABS stays active under every ESP or TCS brake intervention, so a wheel braked for stability never locks.
  4. ABS–TCS interaction: TCS is effectively “ABS in reverse”. It uses the ABS hardware to brake a spinning driven wheel and adds engine torque reduction through CAN. The two never act on the same wheel with conflicting goals: braking (ABS) and driving (TCS) are mutually exclusive situations.
  5. ABS–ESP interaction: during emergency braking in a bend, ABS keeps all wheels steerable. ESP shifts brake force between wheels (e.g. more on the outer front) to correct yaw. In split-μ braking, ESP and ABS limit the yaw moment build-up.
  6. ESP–TCS interaction: while accelerating in a bend, ESP uses TCS channels (torque cut, wheel braking) to correct under- or oversteer.
  7. Other systems: EBD (brake-force distribution), brake assist, hill-hold, ACC, AEB and cruise control also command the same modulator. Wheel-speed data goes over CAN to the engine, transmission, cluster, airbag and navigation ECUs.

Result: shared hardware lowers cost and weight, and coordinated control gives the best combination of stopping distance, traction and stability.

Source lectureKMS · L8 – Electronic Stability Program (AVT_L8.pptx, slides 6, 14–16); L7 – Traction Control System (AVT TCS.pptx, slides 5, 10)
2024 · Q7(c)How does the Electronic Stability Program (ESP) detect understeer and oversteer? Discuss the action of ESP during emergency lane-change maneuvers.10Topic: ESP understeer/oversteer

Detection:

  1. Driver's intention: the steering-angle sensor gives δ, and the wheel-speed sensors give V. The ECU computes the reference yaw rate from a single-track vehicle model: ψ˙ref\dot\psi_{\text{ref}}ψ˙​ref​ = Vδ/(L + KusK_{us}Kus​V²), limited to μg/V.
  2. Actual behaviour: the yaw-rate sensor measures ψ˙actual\dot\psi_{\text{actual}}ψ˙​actual​, and the lateral-acceleration sensor measures aya_{y}ay​. From these and the wheel speeds the ECU estimates the side-slip angle β.
  3. Comparison: ψ˙actual\dot\psi_{\text{actual}}ψ˙​actual​ smaller than ψ˙ref\dot\psi_{\text{ref}}ψ˙​ref​ (the car turns less than steered, front sliding) ⇒ understeer. ψ˙actual\dot\psi_{\text{actual}}ψ˙​actual​ larger than ψ˙ref\dot\psi_{\text{ref}}ψ˙​ref​, or a large or rising β (the rear slides out) ⇒ oversteer.
  4. Correction: understeer ⇒ brake the inner rear wheel and reduce engine torque (yaw moment into the bend). Oversteer ⇒ brake the outer front wheel (counter yaw moment).

ESP action in an emergency lane change (e.g. swerving right to avoid an obstacle, then left back into the lane; lecture figure “right–left cornering sequence”):

  • Phase 1: the driver steers sharply right. Lateral force builds up.
  • Phase 2: the rear starts to break away (incipient oversteer to the right). ESP brakes the left front (outer) wheel, creating a counter yaw moment and stopping the rotation.
  • Phase 3: the driver counter-steers left. Without ESP, the stored yaw energy makes the car swing violently and the driver loses control. With ESP, the vehicle stays under control.
  • Phase 4: in the left turn the rear tends to break away the other way. ESP brakes the right front (now outer) wheel, fully stabilising the car in the original lane.
  • If the driver also brakes, ABS keeps every wheel steerable while ESP varies the brake pressure per wheel. Engine torque is reduced throughout. The car follows the intended path instead of spinning.
Source lectureKMS · L8 – Electronic Stability Program (AVT_L8.pptx, slides 5–11); L8 – Electronic Stability Program (AVT_L8.pptx, slides 13–15)
2023 · Q7(c)Explain: - “Electronic stability program (ESP)” works in conjunction with ABS and TCS to enhance overall vehicle stability.12Topic: ESP with ABS and TCS

The statement is from the lecture. ESP is not a separate box added beside ABS and TCS: it is built on top of them, shares their hardware and uses them as its tools (Figure 6.3, §6.6).

1. Shared hardware. One integrated unit (ECU and hydraulic modulator) and the same four wheel-speed sensors serve all three systems. ABS supplies wheel-speed sensing and pressure reduction. TCS adds active pressure build-up (pump and switching valves) and the CAN link to the engine ECU. ESP adds the steering-angle, yaw-rate, lateral-acceleration and brake-pressure sensors.

2. Division of tasks:

SystemControlsActs whenHow
ABSBrake slip (longitudinal)BrakingHolds and releases pressure so no wheel locks
TCSDrive slip (longitudinal)AcceleratingReduces engine torque, brakes the spinning wheel
ESPYaw rate and side-slip angle (lateral)Any time: braking, accelerating, coasting, corneringBrakes individual wheels and adjusts engine torque to create a correcting yaw moment

3. Layered control. ESP is the top-level controller. It compares the driver's intended path (steering angle and speed → reference yaw rate, (6.1)) with the actual yaw rate and lateral acceleration. When they differ, it decides the yaw moment needed and gives slip targets for individual wheels to the ABS and TCS slip controllers, which carry them out. Because ABS always stays active underneath, a wheel braked by ESP never locks, so it keeps its side grip.

4. Examples:

  • Braking in a bend or in an emergency lane change: ABS keeps every wheel steerable; ESP adds extra brake force at the outer front wheel if the car oversteers, or at the inner rear wheel if it understeers.
  • Accelerating in a bend: TCS stops the driven wheels spinning; ESP additionally reduces engine torque and brakes a wheel if the car starts to slide.
  • Coasting or lifting off: neither ABS nor TCS acts, but ESP can still brake single wheels to stop a skid.

Result: ABS secures longitudinal grip in braking, TCS in acceleration, and ESP adds lateral (yaw) control in every driving condition. Together they keep the vehicle stable, steerable and on the intended path, which greatly reduces loss-of-control accidents.

Source lectureKMS · L8 – Electronic Stability Program (AVT_L8.pptx, slides 6, 13–16)
2023 · Q7(d)Why modern vehicles use ESP?05Topic: need for ESP

Modern vehicles use ESP for these reasons (lecture):

  1. Enhanced vehicle safety: it prevents loss of control, a major cause of serious single-vehicle accidents. Large studies found roughly a third fewer single-vehicle crashes in cars fitted with ESC.
  2. Improved traction and stability: it uses the ABS and TCS functions and adds yaw control in every driving condition.
  3. Mitigation of understeer and oversteer: it compares the actual yaw rate with the driver's intention and brakes the right wheel to correct the car (§6.3).
  4. Effective counteracting of skidding: it reacts within milliseconds, before most drivers notice a skid, for example in sudden evasive manoeuvres or on ice.
  5. Driver confidence and assistance: it helps average drivers keep control in emergencies. It is also the base for other functions such as rollover mitigation and trailer-sway control.

Because of these benefits, ESC is now standard and is legally required on new cars in the USA (from model year 2012) and the EU (from 2014).

Source lectureKMS · L8 – Electronic Stability Program (AVT_L8.pptx, slides 6–7)

7. Hybrid, Electric and Alternative-Fuel Vehicles ★★★

7.1 Hybrid Vehicles: Definition

Definitions (lecture)
Hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) are powered by an internal combustion engine and an electric motor that uses energy stored in batteries. A (conventional) HEV cannot be plugged in to charge the battery. The battery is charged by regenerative braking and by the internal combustion engine. Example: Toyota Prius.

More generally, a hybrid vehicle uses two or more distinct types of power. Examples: an IC engine driving a generator that powers an electric motor (diesel-electric trains), or submarines that run on diesel when surfaced and on batteries when submerged. Other ways to store energy include pressurised fluid in hydraulic hybrids.

Why hybridise? The electric motor is more efficient at producing torque (turning power), especially from standstill, while the combustion engine is better at maintaining high speed. Switching from one to the other at the right time while accelerating gives better energy efficiency. HEVs can be designed for different goals, such as better fuel economy or more power.

7.2 Working Principle: Key HEV Technologies (lecture)

  1. Regenerative braking: recaptures energy normally lost when coasting or braking. The forward motion of the wheels turns the motor, which then works as a generator. This generates electricity that charges the battery, and the generator's drag helps slow the vehicle.
  2. Electric motor drive/assist: the motor adds power to help the engine when accelerating, overtaking or climbing hills. This allows a smaller, more efficient engine. In some hybrids the motor alone propels the vehicle at low speeds, where petrol engines are least efficient.
  3. Automatic start/stop: automatically switches off the engine when the vehicle stops and restarts it when the accelerator is pressed. This reduces the energy wasted by idling.

The lecture figure shows the main parts of a power-split hybrid: battery, internal combustion engine, generator, power-split device (planetary gear set) and electric motor, connected to the drive wheels.

7.3 HEV Architectures

ArchitectureWorkingProsConsExamples
SeriesEngine drives a generator only. Motor alone drives the wheels.Engine runs at its best-efficiency point, simple controlDouble energy conversion losses at highway speed, large motor neededNissan e-Power, diesel-electric trains
ParallelEngine and motor both connected mechanically to the wheels.Efficient at highway speed, small motorEngine speed tied to vehicle speedHonda IMA, many mild hybrids
Series-parallel (power-split)Planetary gear splits engine power between wheels and generator. Motor adds or recovers power.Best of both; works like an e-CVTComplex, costlyToyota Prius, Camry, RAV4 Hybrid

Degree of hybridisation: micro hybrid (start-stop only), mild hybrid (48 V motor assists but cannot drive alone), full hybrid (can drive electrically at low speed), plug-in hybrid (PHEV: larger battery charged from the grid, longer electric range).

Popular hybrid vehicles (lecture): Toyota RAV4 Hybrid, Toyota Corolla Hybrid, Toyota Prius V, Honda Insight Hybrid, Toyota Camry Hybrid, Hyundai Sonata Hybrid.

7.4 Merits and Demerits of Hybrid Vehicles

Advantages

  • Better fuel economy (often 20–40 % better in city driving)
  • Lower CO₂ and pollutant emissions
  • Regenerative braking recovers braking energy
  • Smaller, more efficient engine (downsizing)
  • Instant motor torque gives smooth, strong acceleration
  • Quiet, zero-emission electric driving at low speed
  • No idling losses (start/stop)
  • Less brake wear
  • No range anxiety, unlike a pure EV, and no charging infrastructure needed

Demerits

  • Heavier (lecture): the electric motor, battery pack, regenerative braking system and their cooling systems add weight
  • Higher purchase cost
  • More complex, needs specialised maintenance
  • Battery ageing and replacement cost
  • Smaller fuel-economy advantage on the highway
  • High-voltage safety concerns
  • Less boot space

7.5 Electric Vehicles (EV)

Definition (lecture)
An electric vehicle (EV) uses one or more electric (traction) motors for propulsion. It may be powered through a collector system with electricity from off-vehicle sources (e.g. trolleybuses and trains), or it may be self-contained with a battery, solar panels or an electric generator that converts fuel into electricity. EVs include road and rail vehicles, surface and underwater craft, and electric aircraft and spacecraft.

EVs are getting more attention because of technological developments (cheaper, denser lithium-ion batteries, efficient motors and power electronics) and an increased focus on renewable energy and zero-emission transport. Popular electric cars (lecture): BYD Seal, Tesla Model S, Rolls-Royce Spectre.

Main components of a battery EV: traction battery pack with battery management system (BMS) · inverter (DC → 3-phase AC) · traction motor (PMSM or induction) · single-speed reduction gear and differential · on-board charger and DC fast-charging port · DC-DC converter (high voltage → 12 V) · thermal management · vehicle control unit.

TypeEnergy sourcePlug-in?Electric-only rangeTailpipe emissions
HEVPetrol/diesel + small batteryNo≈ 1–2 km at low speedReduced
PHEVPetrol + medium batteryYes≈ 30–80 kmZero in EV mode
BEVLarge battery onlyYes≈ 250–600 kmZero
FCEVHydrogen + fuel cell (+ buffer battery)No (refuel H₂)≈ 500–650 kmZero (water only)

7.6 Fuel-Cell Vehicles SUPPLEMENTARY

Definition
A fuel-cell electric vehicle (FCEV) is an electric vehicle whose electricity is produced on board by a fuel cell. The fuel cell converts the chemical energy of hydrogen and oxygen from the air directly into electricity, heat and water, without combustion. Examples: Toyota Mirai, Hyundai Nexo.

Working (PEM fuel cell): hydrogen is fed to the anode, where a platinum catalyst splits it into protons and electrons. The proton-exchange membrane lets only the protons through to the cathode. The electrons flow through the external circuit (motor), doing work. At the cathode, protons, electrons and oxygen combine to form water.

Reactions
Anode:   H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻     Cathode:   ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O     Overall:   H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O + electricity + heat
Single-cell voltage ≈ 0.6–0.8 V under load, so hundreds of cells are stacked in series.

Components: high-pressure hydrogen tanks (700 bar) · fuel-cell stack · air compressor/humidifier · DC-DC boost converter · buffer battery (stores regenerative braking energy, covers peak power) · inverter and traction motor · cooling system.

Merits: zero tailpipe emissions (only water), 3–5 minute refuelling, long range, higher efficiency than an IC engine (≈ 50–60 % stack efficiency). Demerits: expensive (platinum catalyst), few hydrogen stations, hydrogen production is often from natural gas, and high-pressure storage raises safety and packaging issues.

7.7 CNG / LPG / Natural Gas Vehicles (NGV) SUPPLEMENTARY

Definition
A natural gas vehicle (NGV) runs its IC engine on natural gas (mainly methane, CH₄), stored on board either as compressed natural gas (CNG, ≈ 200–250 bar) or as liquefied natural gas (LNG, −162 °C). Most cars in Bangladesh are bi-fuel (petrol + CNG) spark-ignition vehicles converted by approved conversion workshops.

7.7.1 Working of a CNG (NGV) system

  1. CNG is filled through the filling (refuelling) valve into high-pressure cylinders at about 200 bar.
  2. When the engine runs on gas, the cylinder valve and a high-pressure solenoid shut-off valve open. Gas flows through the stainless-steel high-pressure pipe to the engine bay.
  3. The pressure regulator (reducer) drops the pressure in stages from ≈ 200 bar to about 1–2 bar (injection systems) or near atmospheric (mixer systems). Gas expansion causes strong cooling, so the regulator is heated by engine coolant to prevent freezing.
  4. The gas is filtered and metered into the engine by gas injectors, controlled by a CNG ECU that uses the petrol ECU's injection signals and a MAP sensor (sequential injection systems), or by a gas-air mixer in the intake (older venturi systems).
  5. In the cylinders, the natural gas–air mixture is ignited by the spark plug as in a petrol engine. Because of methane's high octane number (≈ 120–130) the ignition timing is usually advanced by a timing advance processor.
  6. A fuel selector (changeover) switch on the dashboard switches between petrol and CNG. A pressure gauge / level indicator shows the cylinder contents.
Key componentFunction
CNG cylindersStore gas at ≈ 200 bar. Type 1 (all steel) to Type 4 (full composite). Fitted with a manual valve, a pressure-relief device (PRD: burst disc or fusible plug) and an excess-flow valve.
Filling / refuelling valveReceptacle for the dispenser nozzle, with a non-return valve.
High-pressure pipes and fittingsSeamless stainless-steel tubing carrying high-pressure gas.
Solenoid shut-off valveElectrically opens the gas supply only when the engine is running on CNG. Closes automatically if the engine stops.
Pressure regulatorReduces the pressure from 200 bar to working pressure. Heated by coolant.
Gas injectors / mixerMeter gas into the intake.
CNG ECU, MAP sensor, timing advancerControl gas injection timing and duration and adjust spark timing.
Changeover switch and gaugeDriver selects the fuel. Shows the gas quantity.
Vent hoses / gas-tight housingLead any leaked gas outside the passenger compartment.

LPG vehicles work similarly, but LPG (propane/butane) is stored as a liquid at low pressure (≈ 8–10 bar). A vaporiser-regulator turns it into gas. LPG is heavier than air, so leaks collect at floor level, whereas CNG is lighter than air and disperses upward.

Merits of NGV: cheaper fuel, lower CO, HC, CO₂ and particulate emissions, high octane, clean combustion (longer oil and spark-plug life), abundant domestic supply. Demerits: heavy cylinders reduce payload and boot space, ≈ 10–15 % less power than petrol, shorter range, limited filling stations, and periodic cylinder testing is required.

7.7.2 Maintenance and safety of NGVs

MaintenanceSafety facilities and practices
  • Periodic hydrostatic re-testing of cylinders (typically every 5 years, or as required by the regulatory authority). Cylinders past their certified life are condemned.
  • Regular leak tests of all joints (soap solution or gas detector).
  • Replace the gas filter and inspect the regulator (diaphragm, heating hoses) at the specified intervals.
  • Check spark plugs (higher ignition voltage is needed for CNG) and ignition leads, and set ignition timing.
  • Check the cylinder mounting brackets and straps and look for corrosion or damage.
  • Service and calibrate the injectors and ECU (diagnostics).
  • Only certified workshops should install or repair the kit.
  • Pressure-relief device (burst disc/fusible plug) vents gas safely in a fire so the cylinder does not explode.
  • Excess-flow valve stops gas flow if a pipe ruptures.
  • Solenoid shut-off valves close automatically when the engine stops or the ignition is switched off.
  • Manual shut-off valve for emergencies and servicing.
  • Gas-tight housing and vent lines route leaks outside the cabin.
  • Certified, tested cylinders and fittings (ISO 11439 / NGV standards), with a certificate and fitness sticker.
  • Refuelling: engine off, passengers out, no smoking or flames.
  • Never overfill. Park in ventilated areas. Know the smell of gas (odorant added).

7.8 Regenerative Braking and Electric-Only Propulsion

Principle: when the driver lifts off or brakes, the controller switches the traction motor into generator mode. The wheels drive the motor, which converts the vehicle's kinetic energy into electrical energy. The inverter rectifies it and charges the battery. The generator's electromagnetic torque opposes rotation and slows the vehicle. The brake ECU blends regenerative and friction braking: regeneration is used first, and the friction brakes add force for strong stops, at very low speed, when the battery is full or cold, and when ABS/ESP must act.

Energy recovered
Erec=ηregen×12m(v12−v22)(7.1)E_{\text{rec}}=\eta_{\text{regen}}\times\tfrac12m\left(v_1^2-v_2^2\right)\tag{7.1}Erec​=ηregen​×21​m(v12​−v22​)(7.1) ηregen\eta_{\text{regen}}ηregen​ (wheel → battery) is typically 0.5–0.7 when losses in motor, inverter and battery are included.

Conditions for electric-only propulsion in a (full) hybrid:

  1. Low vehicle speed: typically below ≈ 40–60 km/h, where the engine is least efficient.
  2. Low power demand: gentle acceleration, cruising on the flat or downhill, creeping in traffic. A hard pedal press starts the engine.
  3. Sufficient battery state of charge (SOC) above the controller's lower limit, and battery temperature within limits.
  4. Engine not needed for other reasons: engine and catalyst are warm (no warm-up needed), and heater or defrost demand is low.
  5. Driver selection: the “EV mode” button, where fitted, within the above limits.

7.10 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q8(a)What is a hybrid vehicle and fuel cell vehicle? What are the advantages of hybrid vehicles?10Topic: hybrid · fuel cell

Hybrid vehicle: a vehicle that uses two or more distinct power sources, most commonly an internal combustion engine and an electric motor with a battery (HEV). A conventional HEV cannot be plugged in. Its battery is charged by the engine and by regenerative braking. The motor provides strong low-speed torque and assists the engine during acceleration, while the engine supplies power efficiently at high speed. Key technologies are regenerative braking, electric motor drive/assist and automatic start/stop. Architectures: series, parallel and series-parallel (power-split, e.g. Toyota Prius). Draw Fig. 7.1.

Fuel-cell vehicle (FCEV): an electric vehicle whose electricity is produced on board by a fuel cell stack. The stack combines hydrogen (stored at ≈ 700 bar) with oxygen from the air: anode H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻, cathode ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O. The electrons drive the traction motor through an inverter, and the only exhaust is water. A small buffer battery stores regenerative energy (e.g. Toyota Mirai, Hyundai Nexo).

Advantages of hybrid vehicles: (1) better fuel economy, especially in city traffic; (2) lower CO₂ and pollutant emissions; (3) regenerative braking recovers energy normally lost as heat; (4) a smaller, more efficient engine can be used because the motor assists; (5) quiet, zero-emission electric driving at low speed; (6) no idling losses thanks to start/stop; (7) instant motor torque gives smooth acceleration; (8) less brake wear; (9) unlike pure EVs there is no range anxiety and no need for charging infrastructure. Demerit to mention: heavier (motor, battery, regenerative braking, cooling systems) and more expensive.

Source lectureKMS · L9 – Hybrid & Electric Vehicles (AVT_L9.pptx, slides 4–8) — Fuel-cell vehicles not in slides; see §7.6
2024 · Q8(a)How do Natural Gas Vehicles (NGV) work? Discuss the key components of a natural gas vehicle.10Topic: NGV components

An NGV burns natural gas (mainly methane) in a spark-ignition engine. The gas is stored on board as CNG at ≈ 200–250 bar (or as LNG). Working: (1) gas is filled through the filling valve into high-pressure cylinders; (2) when CNG mode is selected, the cylinder and solenoid valves open and gas flows through high-pressure steel pipes; (3) a coolant-heated pressure regulator reduces the pressure to ≈ 1–2 bar; (4) the CNG ECU meters the gas through injectors (or a mixer) into the intake, based on engine load and speed signals; (5) the air–gas mixture is compressed and spark-ignited as in a petrol engine, with the ignition timing advanced to suit methane's high octane number; (6) a changeover switch lets bi-fuel cars return to petrol. Draw the flow line from §7.7.1.

Key components: CNG cylinders with valve, pressure-relief device and excess-flow valve · filling valve · high-pressure pipes · solenoid shut-off valve · pressure regulator (reducer) · gas filter · injector rail or gas-air mixer · CNG ECU with MAP sensor and timing advancer · fuel changeover switch and pressure gauge · vent and gas-tight housing. (Give one line of function for each, from the table in §7.7.1.)

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §7.7.1)
2024 · Q8(b)Discuss the maintenance and safety facilities of a natural gas vehicle.05Topic: NGV safety

Maintenance: periodic hydrostatic re-testing of cylinders (typically every 5 years) and replacement at end of life; regular leak tests of joints; replacement of the gas filter and inspection of the regulator; checking spark plugs and ignition timing (CNG needs a higher ignition voltage); inspection of cylinder brackets for corrosion and tightness; work done only at certified workshops.

Safety facilities: pressure-relief device (burst disc/fusible plug) to prevent cylinder rupture in a fire; excess-flow valve against pipe rupture; automatic solenoid shut-off when the engine stops; manual shut-off valve; gas-tight housing with vent lines to outside; certified cylinders with fitness certificates; safe refuelling practice (engine off, passengers out, no smoking); and the gas disperses upward because CNG is lighter than air.

Source lectureNot in the slides — answer built from standard theory (see §7.7.2)
2024 · Q8(c)Explain the role of regenerative braking in hybrid vehicles. In hybrid vehicles, under what conditions electric only propulsion is possible?10Topic: regenerative braking

Role of regenerative braking: during deceleration the traction motor is switched to generator mode. The wheels drive it, and it converts kinetic energy (½mv²) into electrical energy that is stored in the battery instead of being wasted as heat in the brakes. Its generator torque also slows the car. The brake ECU blends regenerative and friction braking so that pedal feel stays normal and ABS/ESP keep priority. Benefits: 1) it is the main energy source of a non-plug-in HEV, recharging the battery for later electric driving and motor assist; 2) it improves fuel economy and cuts emissions, especially in stop-and-go traffic; 3) it reduces brake pad and disc wear; 4) it allows one-pedal driving feel. Example: a 1500 kg car stopping from 60 km/h has 208 kJ, of which ≈ 125 kJ (60 %) can be recovered.

Conditions for electric-only propulsion: (1) low speed (≈ below 40–60 km/h depending on the model); (2) low power demand (light throttle, steady cruising, creeping, downhill); (3) battery SOC above its minimum threshold and battery temperature within limits; (4) engine and catalyst already warm and no heavy heating demand, so the engine is not needed; (5) the driver selects EV mode where available. When any of these is not met (hard acceleration, high speed, low SOC), the controller starts the engine.

Source lectureKMS · L9 – Hybrid & Electric Vehicles (AVT_L9.pptx, slides 4, 7)
2023 · Q8(a)What is an electric vehicle (EV)? Outline the differences between an electric vehicle and a hybrid vehicle (HV).10Topic: EV vs hybrid

Electric vehicle (EV): a vehicle that uses one or more electric (traction) motors for propulsion. It is powered either through a collector system from off-vehicle electricity or self-contained with a battery, solar panels or a generator (lecture, §7.5). A battery EV (BEV) has no combustion engine at all: battery pack with BMS, inverter, traction motor, single-speed reduction gear and an on-board charger. A hybrid vehicle combines an internal combustion engine with an electric motor and a battery that is charged by regenerative braking and by the engine (§7.1).

AspectElectric vehicle (BEV)Hybrid vehicle (HEV)
Power sourceBattery onlyPetrol/diesel engine + small battery
PropulsionElectric motor(s) onlyEngine and/or motor (series, parallel or power-split, §7.3)
Energy inputCharged from the grid (plug-in, AC or DC fast charging)Fuel at a filling station; battery charged on board (not plugged in)
Battery sizeLarge (≈ 40–100 kWh)Small (≈ 1–2 kWh)
Tailpipe emissionsZero (no exhaust)Reduced, but not zero
Range and refuelling250–600 km; 20–60 min fast charge, hours at homeLong range (600–1000 km); 3–5 min refuel
Electric-only drivingAlwaysOnly short distances at low speed and load
EfficiencyHighest (≈ 85–90 % battery to wheel)Better than a conventional car, still limited by the engine
Complexity and maintenanceFew moving parts, no oil changesTwo complete powertrains, so more complex
Cost and infrastructureHigh battery cost; needs a charging networkModerate cost; uses the existing fuel network
Examples (lecture)Tesla Model S, BYD Seal, Rolls-Royce SpectreToyota Prius, Corolla Hybrid, Honda Insight

Both recover energy by regenerative braking. A plug-in hybrid (PHEV) lies between the two: a larger battery that is charged from the grid for 30–80 km of electric driving, plus an engine for longer trips.

Working (§7.6). A fuel-cell electric vehicle (FCEV) is an electric car that makes its own electricity on board from hydrogen:

  1. Hydrogen stored in high-pressure tanks (700 bar) is fed to the anode of the PEM fuel-cell stack. Air from a compressor is fed to the cathode.
  2. At the anode a platinum catalyst splits hydrogen: H2→2H++2e−\text{H}_2\to2\text{H}^++2e^-H2​→2H++2e−. The membrane passes only the protons. The electrons flow through the external circuit and do work in the motor.

  4. Each cell gives about 0.6–0.8 V, so hundreds are stacked in series. A DC-DC converter and inverter feed the traction motor. A buffer battery stores regenerative-braking energy and supplies peak power.

Energy conversionElectrochemical, no combustionCombustion of petrol in an IC engine

So the main differences are no combustion, zero tailpipe emissions, electric drive and higher efficiency, at the price of expensive technology and a limited hydrogen supply.
