8. Autonomous Navigation SUPPLEMENTARY ★★★

Note
This topic is in the syllabus (“Autonomous Navigation: perception, localization and mapping, motion planning and motion control; applications to UAVs, automated vehicles and self-driving cars”) and was asked in both 2022 and 2024 Section B, but there is no KMS slide file on it yet. This chapter is written from the standard references so that the whole of Section B is covered.

8.1 Definition and Levels of Automation

Autonomous navigation
Autonomous navigation is a vehicle's ability to travel from its current position to a destination without human control. It must sense its surroundings, understand them (perception), know where it is (localization and mapping), decide where and how to move (planning), and carry out the motion (control), safely and in real time. It applies to self-driving cars, UAVs (drones), mobile robots, and marine and planetary vehicles.
SAE levelNameWho drives / monitorsExample
0No automationDriver does everything (warnings only)Lane-departure warning
1Driver assistanceSystem controls steering or speedACC or lane keeping
2Partial automationSystem steers and controls speed; driver monitors constantlyTesla Autopilot, highway assist
3Conditional automationSystem drives in limited conditions; driver must take over on requestTraffic-jam pilot
4High automationNo driver needed within a defined operating domain (ODD)Robotaxi in a geo-fenced city
5Full automationDrives everywhere, in all conditionsNot yet commercially available

8.2 Architecture of an Autonomous Driving System

8.3 Sensors for Autonomous Driving

SensorPrincipleFunctions in autonomous drivingStrengths / weaknesses
GPS (GNSS)Trilateration from satellite signal travel times. RTK correction gives cm-level accuracy.Global (absolute) position, latitude/longitude; route planning; initialising localization; time synchronisation.Absolute, drift-free. But metre-level error without RTK, lost in tunnels and urban canyons, low update rate (1–10 Hz).
IMU3-axis accelerometers + 3-axis gyroscopes.High-rate (100–1000 Hz) acceleration and angular rate → orientation (roll, pitch, yaw) and dead reckoning between GPS updates; bridges GPS outages; motion compensation for LiDAR and cameras.Fast, works everywhere. But integration error drifts over time.
GPS + IMU are fused (Kalman filter): GPS corrects the IMU drift and the IMU fills gaps between and during GPS outages, giving a smooth, accurate position, velocity and heading.
LiDARLaser pulses; time-of-flight gives distance. Rotating or solid-state scanning builds a 3-D point cloud.Precise 3-D mapping of surroundings; detection and range of obstacles, vehicles and pedestrians; free-space and curb detection; localization by matching scans to HD maps; SLAM.cm-accurate depth, works in darkness. But costly, degraded by heavy rain, fog and snow, gives no colour or texture.
CamerasCMOS image sensors (mono, stereo, surround).Rich semantic information: lane markings, traffic signs and lights (colour), object classification (car, pedestrian, cyclist), free space; depth from stereo or deep learning; driver monitoring.Cheap, high resolution, sees colour and text. But affected by lighting, glare and weather; depth is less accurate.
RadarRadio waves (77 GHz); range and Doppler velocity.Range and relative speed of vehicles ahead (ACC, AEB); works in all weather.Robust in weather, measures velocity directly. Low angular resolution.
UltrasonicSound echo.Short-range (< 5 m) parking and low-speed manoeuvring.Cheap. Very short range.

8.4 Perception

Definition
Perception is the process by which an autonomous vehicle interprets raw sensor data to build an understanding of its environment: what is around it, where it is and how it is moving. It answers questions such as “Where are the lanes? Where are the other cars and pedestrians, and where will they go? Is the traffic light red? Where is the drivable space?”

Perception tasks: (1) object detection and classification (vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists, animals); (2) lane and road-boundary detection; (3) traffic sign and traffic-light recognition; (4) free-space (drivable area) and semantic segmentation; (5) depth and 3-D bounding-box estimation; (6) multi-object tracking over time; (7) motion prediction of other road users; (8) sensor fusion: camera, LiDAR and radar data are combined (early, feature-level or late fusion) so that the weaknesses of one sensor are covered by another. Techniques: convolutional neural networks (YOLO, Faster R-CNN), segmentation networks, point-cloud networks (PointNet, PointPillars), bird's-eye-view (BEV) transformers, and Kalman-filter tracking.

8.5 Localization and Mapping

  • GNSS/IMU fusion: an extended Kalman filter predicts the pose from the IMU (and wheel odometry) and corrects it with GPS fixes, giving position, velocity and heading at high rate.
  • Map-based localization: the vehicle carries a pre-built HD map (cm-accurate lanes, curbs, signs, 3-D point cloud). Live LiDAR scans or camera features are matched to the map (ICP, NDT scan matching, landmark matching, particle filter) to estimate the pose to within ≈ 10 cm.
  • SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping): in unknown areas the vehicle or robot builds the map while localizing itself in it (e.g. LiDAR SLAM, visual SLAM such as ORB-SLAM). Loop closure corrects accumulated drift.
  • Mapping also means keeping a dynamic local map (occupancy grid or BEV map) of obstacles around the vehicle for planning.

8.5.1 Localization with GPS and IMU only (GNSS/INS fusion)

A GPS (GNSS) receiver gives an absolute position and velocity, but only 1–10 times per second, with an error of about 2–5 m (worse near buildings), and it can be lost completely in tunnels. An IMU (three accelerometers and three gyroscopes) gives accelerations and turn rates 100–1000 times per second. Integrating them (dead reckoning) gives a smooth, fast pose, but every small sensor bias is integrated too, so the error grows without limit. The two sensors fail in opposite ways, so they are combined with a Kalman filter (Figure 8.2):

Kalman filter: predict with the IMU, update with GPS
State, e.g. x=[x, y, vx, vy, ψ, ba, bg]T\mathbf x=[x,\ y,\ v_x,\ v_y,\ \psi,\ b_a,\ b_g]^Tx=[x, y, vx​, vy​, ψ, ba​, bg​]T (position, velocity, heading, accelerometer and gyro biases). Predict (every IMU sample):x^k∣k−1=f(x^k−1, ak, ωk),Pk∣k−1=FPk−1FT+Q\text{Predict (every IMU sample):}\quad \hat{\mathbf x}_{k|k-1}=f(\hat{\mathbf x}_{k-1},\,\mathbf a_k,\,\boldsymbol\omega_k),\qquad P_{k|k-1}=F P_{k-1}F^T+QPredict (every IMU sample):x^k∣k−1​=f(x^k−1​,ak​,ωk​),Pk∣k−1​=FPk−1​FT+Q Update (when a GPS fix zk arrives):K=Pk∣k−1HT(HPk∣k−1HT+R)−1\text{Update (when a GPS fix } \mathbf z_k \text{ arrives):}\quad K=P_{k|k-1}H^T\left(HP_{k|k-1}H^T+R\right)^{-1}Update (when a GPS fix zk​ arrives):K=Pk∣k−1​HT(HPk∣k−1​HT+R)−1 x^k=x^k∣k−1+K(zk−Hx^k∣k−1),Pk=(I−KH)Pk∣k−1\hat{\mathbf x}_k=\hat{\mathbf x}_{k|k-1}+K\left(\mathbf z_k-H\hat{\mathbf x}_{k|k-1}\right),\qquad P_k=(I-KH)P_{k|k-1}x^k​=x^k∣k−1​+K(zk​−Hx^k∣k−1​),Pk​=(I−KH)Pk∣k−1​ QQQ = IMU noise, RRR = GPS noise. The gain KKK weights the GPS fix against the prediction; because the biases are in the state, the filter also calibrates the IMU while GPS is available.

Why the IMU alone drifts. A constant accelerometer bias bab_aba​ gives a position error e(t)=12bat2e(t)=\tfrac12b_at^2e(t)=21​ba​t2. Even a small bias of 0.01 m/s² gives 12×0.01×302=4.5\tfrac12\times0.01\times30^2=4.521​×0.01×302=4.5 m after a 30 s GPS outage, and 18 m after 60 s.

8.6 Path/Motion Planning and Motion Control

Planning is hierarchical:

  1. Route (mission) planning: finds the best road route from start to destination on a road-network graph (Dijkstra, A*), as in navigation apps.
  2. Behaviour planning (decision making): decides the manoeuvre from traffic rules and the situation: follow lane, change lane, overtake, stop at a light, yield. Implemented with finite-state machines, rule bases or learning-based policies.
  3. Motion (trajectory) planning: generates a smooth, collision-free, dynamically feasible trajectory (path + speed profile) for the next few seconds. Methods: graph search (A*, Hybrid A*), sampling (RRT, RRT*), state lattices, and optimisation or MPC that minimises a cost of comfort, progress and safety subject to obstacle and vehicle constraints.

Motion control tracks the planned trajectory by commanding steering, throttle and brakes: lateral control with pure pursuit, the Stanley controller or MPC; longitudinal control with PID or MPC for speed and distance. The actuators are drive-by-wire systems (EPS, electronic throttle, brake-by-wire), which is where ESP, ABS and cruise-control technology is reused.

Applications to UAVs: the same pipeline applies in 3-D. GPS/IMU plus barometer and visual odometry give localization. Cameras and LiDAR detect obstacles. 3-D planners (RRT*, A* on voxel grids) plan paths, and flight controllers (cascaded PID on attitude and position) track them. Uses include delivery, inspection, mapping, agriculture and search and rescue.

8.7 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q8(b)What do you mean by Autonomous Navigation? What are the functions of the following in sensing for autonomous driving: (i) GPS/IMU, (ii) LiDAR, and (iii) Cameras.15Topic: autonomous sensing

Autonomous navigation is the ability of a vehicle (car, UAV, robot) to move from its current location to a destination without human control. It does this by sensing its environment, perceiving and understanding it, localizing itself on a map, planning a safe path and trajectory, and controlling steering, throttle and brakes to follow it (draw the pipeline of §8.2). SAE defines levels 0–5 of driving automation.

(i) GPS/IMU: GPS (GNSS) gives the absolute global position (latitude, longitude, altitude) and time by satellite trilateration, and is used for route planning and initial localization. RTK corrections improve it to cm level. The IMU (3-axis accelerometers and gyroscopes) measures linear acceleration and angular rate at high frequency, giving the vehicle's orientation (roll, pitch, yaw), velocity and short-term position by dead reckoning. The two are fused with a Kalman filter: GPS removes the IMU's drift, and the IMU provides smooth, high-rate updates and bridges GPS outages in tunnels and urban canyons. The IMU also motion-compensates LiDAR and camera data.

(ii) LiDAR: emits laser pulses and measures their time of flight to produce a precise 3-D point cloud of the surroundings. Functions: accurate distance and shape of obstacles, vehicles, pedestrians and curbs; free-space detection; 3-D object detection and tracking; building HD maps and localizing the car by matching live scans to the map (SLAM). It works in darkness, but it is expensive and degraded by heavy rain, fog and snow.

(iii) Cameras: provide high-resolution colour images that give semantic information. Functions: detecting and reading lane markings, traffic signs and traffic-light colours; classifying objects (car, truck, pedestrian, cyclist); estimating depth with stereo cameras or deep learning; surround-view parking; driver monitoring. They are cheap and information-rich but sensitive to lighting and weather, so they are fused with LiDAR and radar for robustness.

Source lectureNot in the slides — built from standard theory (see §8.1, §8.3)
2022 · Q8(c)Briefly explain the term ‘Perception’ in context of autonomous driving. How Localization and Path Planning are achieved during autonomous driving?10Topic: perception · localization · planning

Perception is the interpretation of raw sensor data (camera, LiDAR, radar) to build an understanding of the environment: detecting and classifying objects, finding lanes and drivable space, recognising signs and lights, tracking moving objects and predicting their motion. Deep neural networks and sensor fusion are used so that the vehicle “knows what is around it”.

Localization (where am I?) is achieved by: (1) GNSS + IMU + wheel odometry fusion with an extended Kalman filter, giving position and heading; (2) map matching, where LiDAR point clouds or camera landmarks are matched to a pre-built HD map (ICP/NDT scan matching, particle filters) for ≈ 10 cm accuracy; (3) SLAM in unmapped areas, building the map and localizing at the same time.

Path planning (how do I get there?) is achieved hierarchically: (1) route planning on the road graph with Dijkstra or A*; (2) behaviour planning, deciding manoeuvres (lane change, stop, yield) with state machines or rules; (3) motion/trajectory planning, generating a smooth, collision-free path and speed profile with A*/Hybrid A*, RRT*, lattice planners or MPC optimisation, taking account of obstacles, predictions, comfort and vehicle dynamics. The trajectory is then tracked by motion controllers (pure pursuit, Stanley or MPC for steering; PID for speed).

Source lectureNot in the slides — built from standard theory (see §8.4–8.6)
2024 · Q8(d)Suppose you are assigned to develop an autonomous driving system. Your work is to build a deep learning framework for this system. Now, accomplish this task. What are the possible challenges to accomplish this task?10Topic: deep-learning driving system

Development steps of a deep-learning framework:

  1. Define the scope (ODD): e.g. SAE Level 2+/4 highway or urban driving, and the tasks: detection, lane, segmentation, prediction, planning.
  2. Sensor suite and data collection: fit cameras, LiDAR, radar and GPS/IMU, time-synchronised and calibrated. Record large, diverse datasets (day/night, rain, different cities) and supplement with public datasets (KITTI, nuScenes, Waymo) and simulation (CARLA).
  3. Annotation: label 2-D/3-D bounding boxes, lanes, segmentation masks and trajectories, using auto-labelling with human review.
  4. Model design:
    • Perception: CNN backbone (ResNet/EfficientNet) with detection heads (YOLO/Faster R-CNN); PointPillars for LiDAR; multi-sensor BEV fusion network (transformer) outputting objects, lanes and occupancy.
    • Tracking and prediction: Kalman tracker plus a learned trajectory predictor (LSTM/transformer).
    • Planning: learned planner or imitation learning (optionally end-to-end), with a rule-based safety layer that checks the output.
  5. Training: GPU clusters with frameworks such as PyTorch/TensorFlow; data augmentation; multi-task loss; hyper-parameter tuning.
  6. Validation: metrics (mAP, IoU, ADE/FDE), then simulation testing, hardware-in-the-loop, closed-track and finally road testing with a safety driver.
  7. Deployment: optimise (quantisation, pruning, TensorRT) for an automotive-grade embedded computer (e.g. NVIDIA DRIVE) to meet real-time latency (< 100 ms). Integrate with the control and actuator layers (steering, throttle, brake-by-wire).
  8. Continuous improvement (data engine): collect failure cases from the fleet, relabel, retrain and update over the air.

Possible challenges: (1) huge data and labelling cost; (2) long-tail edge cases (rare events, unusual objects, construction zones); (3) adverse weather and lighting (rain, fog, night glare) degrading sensors; (4) domain shift between cities, countries and seasons (e.g. mixed traffic and rickshaws in Bangladesh); (5) real-time computation on limited in-car hardware and power; (6) safety verification and certification (ISO 26262, SOTIF ISO 21448) of black-box networks; (7) lack of interpretability and explainability; (8) adversarial attacks and cybersecurity; (9) sensor calibration and synchronisation; (10) predicting human behaviour and handling interaction; (11) legal, ethical and liability issues; (12) HD-map creation and maintenance.

Source lectureNot in the slides — built from standard theory (see §8.2)
2023 · Q8(b)What is meant by autonomous driving? Suppose, you have to develop a localization system for autonomous driving and you only have GPS and IMU. How will you accomplish this task? State the drawbacks of your developed localization system.15Topic: GPS/IMU localization

Autonomous driving means that the vehicle senses its environment and drives itself — perceiving, localizing, planning and controlling — with little or no human input. SAE defines levels 0 (no automation) to 5 (full automation in all conditions) (§8.1). Localization is the task of knowing where the vehicle is (position, heading, velocity), and every later step depends on it.

Design of the GPS + IMU localization system (§8.5.1, Figure 8.2):

  1. Sensors and mounting: a GNSS receiver (multi-constellation GPS/Galileo/GLONASS, with antenna on the roof) gives position and velocity at 1–10 Hz. A 6-axis IMU (3 accelerometers + 3 gyroscopes) near the vehicle's centre of gravity gives acceleration and turn rate at 100–1000 Hz. Calibrate the IMU's alignment and the lever arm between antenna and IMU.
  2. Time synchronisation and coordinate frames: time-stamp both sensors (GPS PPS signal) and convert GPS latitude/longitude into a local east-north-up frame.
  3. Prediction (dead reckoning): at every IMU sample, rotate the measured acceleration into the navigation frame using the attitude from the integrated gyro rates, subtract gravity and integrate twice to get velocity and position. This gives a smooth, high-rate estimate.
  4. Correction (Kalman filter update): when a GPS fix arrives, the filter compares it with the predicted position and corrects the state with the Kalman gain, weighting each source by its noise (QQQ for the IMU, RRR for GPS). The state includes the IMU biases, so the filter calibrates the IMU while GPS is good. An extended Kalman filter (EKF) is used because the motion equations are nonlinear. In a loosely coupled design, GPS positions are fused; in a tightly coupled design, raw satellite ranges are fused, which still works with fewer than four satellites.
  5. Output: position, velocity, heading and attitude at IMU rate (e.g. 100 Hz) with an accuracy estimate (covariance PPP) for the planner. Check innovations to reject bad GPS fixes (multipath).

Drawbacks of the GPS + IMU system:

  1. Limited accuracy: standard GPS gives 2–5 m, but staying in a lane needs about 10–20 cm. It is not lane-level without RTK corrections.
  2. GPS outages and multipath: in tunnels, parking garages, under bridges and between tall buildings the signal is lost or reflected, so the position jumps or is missing.
  3. IMU drift: during an outage only dead reckoning remains, and the error grows with time squared. A 0.01 m/s² bias gives 4.5 m after 30 s (§8.5.1). Low-cost MEMS IMUs drift even faster.
  4. Heading at standstill or low speed is poorly observable from GPS, and gyro heading drifts.
  5. No knowledge of the surroundings: GPS/IMU tells where the car is on the Earth, not where it is relative to the lane, kerb or obstacles, and it does not detect map changes.
  6. Vulnerable to jamming and spoofing, and the vertical (altitude) accuracy is poor, so multi-level roads are hard to separate.

Remedies: RTK-GNSS for centimetre accuracy, wheel odometry and steering angle as extra inputs, and map matching with LiDAR or camera features against an HD map (or SLAM) for lane-level, outage-tolerant localization (§8.5).
